speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: RIGHT HON. C. D. HOWE APPOINTMENT TO HIS MAJESTY'S PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Before the proceedings of the day are entered upon I should like to refer to a matter which I am sure will be of interest to every member of this house. I refer to a report in the morning press that one of our number has been distinctly honoured since we met here yesterday. I wish to take this opportunity on behalf of my associates and myself, and on this occasion I think I can speak for every member of the house, of extending to the Right Honourable Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) our sincere congratulations.
We regard it occasionally as a privilege, sometimes as a right, always as a responsibility, to tell the minister how he can do his job much better than he has done it before or is doing it now. But on an occasion like this, when his war-time service has been recognized by the crown and when it has been expressed in his appointment to the high position of member of the king's privy council, it is one time when we can extend to him our warmest congratulations on this recognition

of a war-time task well done. I make these comments whole-heartedly on behalf of every member of this group and, I would like to think, of every member of the house. It is an outstanding honour which has come to one of our members, an honour which is richly deserved.

maintopic: RIGHT HON. C. D. HOWE APPOINTMENT TO HIS MAJESTY'S PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like on behalf of this party to associate myself with the words of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). We may not always agree with the minister in some of the policies which he is placing before the house or has placed before the house in days past. But I think we all recognize that the distinction conferred upon him to-day is a mark of the appreciation not only of Canada but of the British commonwealth of the remarkable services which he made to the common cause during the war.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the members of my group would want me to join with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) in expressing our sincere and warm congratulations to the right hon. gentleman who has been distinctly honoured by being made a member of the king's privy council. It is not inconceivable, sir, that the contribution of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply during the time that he was also the minister of munitions during the war was responsible for the victory of the united nations. I think that that is quite possible. While, as the other two gentlemen have said, we may not always have agreed with the things done by the right hon. gentleman, we must admit that all he does is done with a whole heart and a good spirit and with real intent; and we congratulate him upon his success and upon the signal honour which has come to him.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the leaders of the opposition parties for their very kind words on this occasion. UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Mae-

Nicol), the adjournment of the house under standing order 31 for the purpose of discussing a definite emergency, a matter of great and urgent public importance, namely, the United States embargo on coal, issued on June 11 to the Ore and Coal Exchange of Cleveland and on account of the great lakes shipping strike, which embargo was temporarily suspended, and also the tie-up of nearly 25,000 hopper coal cars at United States lake ports ready to unload coal for Canada to Canadian ships, and to discuss the grave peril of drastic shortages of supply to Canadian homes without any supply whatever, especially in central Canada next fall and winter, and the urgent need of an all-Canadian national coal policy accordingly.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I am not quite sure that this is a matter of urgent public importance, but of course, under standing order 31, if twenty members rise the hon. member may proceed.
And leave having been granted:

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I shall not detain the house for more than a few minutes. I first brought up this important question of a national fuel supply and a national policy for Canada on March 19, 1923. I am not going to repeat now what I said at that time, and what I have reiterated several times since, but I wish to impress upon the government the gravity of 1 he present situation, especially to central Canada. An opportunity will be afforded me, I have no doubt, under the main estimates to go into this matter more fully, but at the moment-

speechtext:
Louder? Well, Mr. Speaker, I am not going to speak for more than five minutes this afternoon, and I want to impress the importance of this matter on the government and on the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. By the way, I knew him when he was a young engineer and I should like to congratulate him now on the honour that has come to him. To come back to the coal question, we are faced with the most awful winter that Canada will ever have experienced. I have urged upon the government from time to time the importance of a national fuel policy. According to the latest reports we have received, we shall be shut out from the United States this winter by embargo as far as a coal supply is concerned. Geologists there say that they have a supply for seventy-five years, and I do not think that Canadians should depend further upon the United States for their coal. Thousands of cars are tied up in the United

Coal-Embargo
States-twenty	or twenty-five thousand
American cars at lake Erie ports-and I suggest that the time has come for us to take action and move them. In Alberta and in the maritime provinces, I suggest, lies the solution to our problem, through a national fuel policy. Although, as I have said, I first brought this matter to the attention of the house on March 19, 1923, little has been done about it by the government. The problem is largely one of transportation, and the shortages are in the central provinces, in which there are no coal deposits. The east should move coal as far west as possible; Alberta should move it as far east as it can, and it is for the government now to take active steps to solve the problem by a national supply.
I would ask the hon. gentleman who is seconding the motion to say a few words on the subject.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) deserves the unstinted praise of the whole country for his energy and foresight in bringing this resolution before the house, and Your Honour also deserves unstinted praise for allowing it to 'be presented for discussion. I wish also to thank the house for allowing it to be discussed.
Before I proceed to address a few words to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) may I pause to congratulate him personally upon the high honour that has been conferred upon him. I have said on many occasions across the floor of the house that he is one minister who invariably knows what he is talking about, who knows all the answers; he has a vast fund of information such as few other men in this house can draw upon. Once more I congratulate him sincerely on the high honour that has been conferred upon him.
A few days ago the minister made this statement, as quoted in this morning's Globe and Mail of Toronto, which brings it up to date:
Unless the production and transportation of coal is resumed in the United States in the near future, the central provinces of Canada are faced with nothing less than a calamity, and our people and our industries may be faced with hardship and distress on a scale never experienced during the war years.
That announcement by the right hon. gentleman has caused in my part of the country very grave anxiety over the possible experience next winter. It was quite right that he should warn the people of the calamity that is facing them, and it devolves upon the whole House of Commons to see
that that threatened calamity is averted, or at least the severity of fuel conditions mitigated as far as possible.
We take up a lot of time in this house on matters of little or no importance, the decision of which is of little consequence to the people, but here is something that is of colossal import to everyone. When I was last at home I went to my old coal dealer and was informed that it was useless leaving my order for coal. I have quite a number of buildings and the comfort of their tenants depends upon me. For their safety I may have to order oil burners. In my own home I have" to take out two boilers and have them replaced with a single boiler equipped as an oil burner. I do not mind doing that, but everybody cannot do it. In my own section of the city there is a large working-class population. It would be certainly financially impossible, for one out of twenty-five to buy an oil burner. They have to burn coal. It is a tremendous problem for these humble homes, in which from ninety to ninety-five per cent of the population reside. They will be the sufferers if they cannot get coal. The other five or ten per cent may be able to purchase oil burners. If they are able to obtain the oil they will not suffer, but the great mass of Canadians, particularly in Ontario and Quebec, which provinces have no coal of their own, are in jeopardy.
I am sorry to learn that the anticipated production of coal in the lignite area of northern Ontario is not to be had. It has been found that the moisture content of the lignite coal there is so great that the cost of production would far exceed the value received. That will be a serious blow to northern Ontario, because, as the hon. member for Timiskaming will say if he speaks on this subject, they have been expecting to get coal from northern Ontario. Therefore from whatever point of view it is considered it is a serious problem and a great menace to Ontario people.
I am now going to speak particularly for the people of Toronto. In Toronto we have an energetic mayor. He is always keenly alive to the best interests of the people. A few days ago he issued a solemn warning which can be found in the Toronto Telegram of June 7, as follows:
The mayor pointed out that last year, to June 6, eighty-six coal-carrying ships had docked in Toronto harbour, with 418,849 tons of coal. This year to date, only twenty-six ships have arrived with 97,440 tons, a loss to date of 321,409 tons.
This is a most serious threat to the comfort of the people of that city during next fall and winter. Within three months time
Coal-Embargo

we shall start burning coal in Toronto. The month of June is half gone. How many homes in Toronto have coal I do not know; I have not any, I could not get it. The great majority of homes in Toronto are without coal, and within three months we shall have to start burning it, because many of the homes in that city are heated in the winter with hot water. That system of heating has the reverse effect in the fall months if the heat is not on. The radiators, being full of cold water, will cool the house down to an almost unbearable degree. Therefore it is a matter of vital importance to these people. The minister is probably doing all he can with the staff under his control, but we have to do more than that. What more can be done at the moment I do not know.
Yesterday the coal controller issued a statement in which he said, according to the Toronto Globe:
The shortage in the central provinces this winter is estimated at somewhere near 5,500,000 tons.
This is a serious problem for the people in the central provinces of Quebec and Ontario. I wonder if hon. members realize what it means for the two provinces to be short
5,500,000	tons of coal. It has been said by some that we might use hydro-electric power. Well, the hydro commission in Toronto issued a statement in which they said that to heat five per cent of Toronto homes would require one-third of the hydro power, which is somewhere in the neighbourhood of two and a half to three million horse-power. It would mean that if the homes of Toronto and environs were to be heated by electricity, one-third of all the power that hydro has would heat only fifteen per cent of all the homes.
I am not going to proceed at any length. I am sure that what will be said by the mover and what will be said by the hon. members will attract the attention of this house. That is what we must do-attract the attention of the house to the serious threat to the health of the people of these two great central provinces-I shall not speak of the other provinces at the moment-I certainly will support the minister in anything he can do to expedite shipments of coal and its delivery to the dealers in Ontario and Quebec.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
There is no doubt about the seriousness of the matter raised by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), but in reading the document that he passed to Your Honour I find that he has it chewed up in such a fashion that it is difficult to understand exactly what subject he wants action on at the moment.

The seriousness of the coal situation in Canada did not develop yesterday or the day before. It has been slowly developing over the last twenty years, and it has been heading inevitably toward what we have at the present time.
In his motion the hon. member for ..Broadview deplores the fact that the United States has placed an embargo on coal. I would not expect them to do anything else. The people of the United States have developed their own resource to take care of their own requirements. In addition, in the last three or four years they have been exporting twenty million odd tons of coal to Canada to help us out. It is an indictment against us. We should not scream because the United States government is protecting its own people in their fuel requirements. The indictment in the statement made by the hon. member for Broadview is against ourselves, in that although, a nation of eleven million people, are in possession of one-half of the north American continent, which has as great fuel resources as has the United States, we have neglected to develop our own resource to meet the requirements of our own people. I have no argument or quarrel with the United States government for seeing that the requirements of its own people are met at this time.
As to overcoming this fuel shortage, I do not expect the minister to do it, because you cannot cure in a short time a disease that has been growing for more than twenty years under both Liberal and Conservative administrations. For the last twenty years particularly I remember pilgrimage after pilgrimage leaving the mining areas, both east and west, and converging upon Ottawa with briefs, the preparation of which cost a great deal of money, pointing out to both Conservative and Liberal administrations the situation which was slowly developing and indicating that the time was approaching when, if Canada did not expand her own resources, we could not expect to lean on the United States. I have said that in this house many times during the last five years. The mechanics of a national fuel policy have been set out time and again by representatives of the miners' union, by provincial governments and by interested citizens. Unfortunately all these submissions went to the archives, and nothing was done.
In my opinion the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) is helpless to do very much at this time. You cannot develop a -mine overnight; you cannot increase production in old, worn out mines. In the beginning of the last war the recommendation was advanced in this house, and in briefs submitted to the government, that new development

should be undertaken in the coal fields. That requires a large capital outlay. The present operators are not going to spend the money; they have made this abundantly clear. No agency in Canada, other than the government, is going to tackle that problem and make the capital expenditure necessary to increase both the quantity and quality of fuel available in this country. The government cannot meet the present emergency, either, because I do not think production can be stepped up in the industry as it exists at present. A royal commission has been set up to study this question, and by this time I suppose that commission knows more than anyone else in Canada about the possibility of increasing production and the problems of marketing our coal. I suggest to the minister that he get in touch with the personnel of that commission and ask for an interim report on the possibility of getting additional production. I do not expect the minister to be able to do anything about it. I do not know what the royal commission would suggest, but I see no possible chance of improving the situation to any great extent from Canadian production; so if we are to depend upon our own production this year a great many people in Canada will go cold. The only solution is to get assistance from the United States, as we have done in the past.
The hon. member for Broadview also points out that some fuel is available in the Untied States, but that because of the strike on the great lakes that coal cannot be brought across to Canada. As I understand the hon. gentleman's motion, there are some 25,000 cars at lake ports. I am not going into the merits or demerits of that strike on the great lakes, though I will say that it too is the result of neglect. I do not think the strike on the great lakes ever should have developed. The only question at issue there is the establishment of an eight-hour day, something every other classification of worker on this continent secured many years ago by .legislation.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Well, if there were enough C.C.F. governments in the world, there would not be any war. There would be no hungry people, no poverty and insecurity, and no reason to go to war. I say to the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), in a kindly way, that the matter has been neglected. As I said a moment ago, most of the other workers on this continent have the eight-hour day by legislation, and have had it for a long time.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Coal miners should have it. Why haven't they?

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: They have it.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: What about the fishermen and farmers?

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: They regulate their own hours; there is no boss over them with a whip. If a farmer or fisherman wants to get up at four o'clock in the morning, that is up to him. In the field of industry, however, legislation is possible, and the seamen come within that category. I think back in 1919 or 1920 the Canadian government signified by an international understanding that it was favourable to an eight-hour day for seamen. The only point at issue in t'he seamen's strike is the granting of an eight-hour day and the establishment of a three-watch system on the boats.

problem at, issue in the strike. If that question could be satisfactorily dealt with, I believe the other matters of wages and so forth could be ironed out without great difficulty. When

Hon. gentlemen to my right had a chance to do something about it from 1930 to 1935, but they neglected it also. In addition to the government not having implemented that international understanding, however, there is t'he problem of our present labour legislation. A few days ago the minister stated-

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I have read the motion very carefully, Mr. Speaker, and I am following it clause by clause. As I said when I rose, the motion is so badly twisted that it is difficult to understand exactly what is required. I do not blame you, Mr. Speaker, for being confused. When I discuss a subject I always try to speak with relevance to that subject. I have read carefully the part of the motion which deals with the embargo-the preamble, one might call it-and I am trying to follow the suggestion contained in the hon. member's motion that there are certain reasons for the shortage of fuel in Canada. The hon. member says this:
The United States embargo on coal, issued on June 11, to the ore and eoai exchange of Cleveland, and on account of the great lakes shipping strike-
That is it.
-which embargo was temporarily suspended, and also the tie-up of nearly 25,000 hopper coal cars at United States lake ports.
One would get the impression that the hon. member for Broadview is telling the house that there are 25,000 cars of coal on the other side of the border which could be made available to the country if the strike on the great lakes were settled. If that is so, 1, believe I am in order in discussing the relevancy of that strike to the Canadian fuel situation, and in suggesting to the minister ways and means

whereby the strike might be avoided and settled, in order to get the coal into Canada by ships.
I had begun to point out to the minister that I believe much of our difficulty to-day in the field of labour has arisen from the fact that there have grown up in Canada during the war a series of emergency measures in respect of labour which, while applicable during the time of war, after the termination of hostilities are not suitable, because we are now facing a completely new problem. The mechanics available in the Department of Labour to-day for the settlement of disputes should be revamped to meet the new conditions. Instead of having to go through all the ramifications of war labour boards, there should be a shorter cut. Those boards create antagonism in the minds of the workers, with the result that we have upheaval. I say the time has come when the Minister of Labour should consider seriously the abandonment of regional and national war labour boards. Instead of having that kind of machinery the minister should have regional and national industrial councils, with equal representation from employers, employees and governments. Then instead of the seamen or the steelworkers or any other group employed on certain specific jobs having to sit down and talk to the members of a war labour board, the chairman of which may have studied law and may be most competent in his own field, but who does not understand judging the merits or demerits of a dispute, they would discuss the matter with those more competent to judge.
In my opinion many of the decisions made to-day are faulty because the problems are not well understood. The minister knows these problems, and I believe if he were meeting with those who have specific grievances, together with representatives from industry and from his own department, he could sit around a table with them and could understand what was being said. Each group would understand what the other was talking about.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I just completed a four-hour session before coming to the house to-day, and I have been doing that every day all week.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Yes, but the minister does not make any decisions. His decisions must go back to the national war labour board. I call the minister's attention to the Sydney plant, and the five-cent differential in rate. I know he would have granted that five cents four years ago. But he has not the power; the matter has to go back to the national

Coal-Embargo
war labour board. They rejected it again last week-after four years of discussion. And we wonder why there is trouble!
I am suggesting to the minister the time has come when he should accept more responsibility, by meeting with those concerned, dealing with both sides, talking bluntly and with common sense, to find out which side may be at fault. If that had been done five or six months ago with the Canadian seamen, we would not be confronted now with a strike on the great lakes to-day, and would not be relating that strike to the shortage of fuel in Canada. I ask the minister to consider that seriously.
I believe this strike could be settled; it should have been settled long ago. I do not see how any employer in this country can be permitted to sit down and say, "I am going to tie up the ships on the great lakes because I do not w'ant to recognize an organization, and I do not want to grant an eight hour day to my employees." That is not his prerogative; it is the prerogative of the Canadian government. The eight hour day has been an accepted principle throughout the continent-and was accepted many years ago. When an employer takes the dog-in-the-manger attitude, then I say he is defying the accepted laws of the country. He is being unfair with anyone who is trying to deal fairly with him.
On the other hand if the Minister of Labour, or the government, as indicated a few days ago by the minister, believes that a small group in the leadership of any organization is taking advantage of the fact that the membership are not as well posted as their leaders, and if the minister and government feel that such leaders are manipulating those organizations for political purposes or for their own purposes, then I say the minister should be just as frank with that small group guilty of disruption of production as he would be to the other side. There cannot be any middle-of-the-road policy in a matter of this kind. Neither should one use the big stick on one section and refuse to use it on the other. If the minister takes the position that he is going to be fair to both sides, then he should use the same language to both sides. If the minister believed for a minute that the union was at fault, he should tell them so, and should tell them what they should do. On the other hand he should also tell the employers and owners what they should do, when they say the eight-hour day is not going to be accepted. Let him tell those people that the eight-hour day is accepted, and that it is time they got in line. Let him say: You will fall in with it, or we will put a con-63260-155
troller in and take over your business, so that you can have an opportunity to study labour legislation which has been in existence in other parts of the world for many years.
I am not going to occupy more of the time of the house. I leave with the minister this suggestion, that the time has come when he should be facing the situation squarely, when he should be changing existing laws which in my opinion are promoting strikes. Let him be fair to both sides, if it is in the best interests of the people of Canada. Let him not pull his punches when talking to either side; and if he does that, I believe the Canadian people will support him.
I am sorry to find the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply facing this problem. It pleased me to see that he received some recognition for services rendered by him during the war. My experience in dealing with him has been that he wants to get things done. In this instance, however, he has inherited a problem that has been developing for twenty years, and has now reached a point where there is no easy or early solution.
The minister might as well take time by the forelock and make a large appropriation of money to deal with this matter. Let him tap some of the potentially rich seams in Canada, so that we may get ready for the next generation, and will not be left at the mercy of the United States, when they put on an embargo to protect their own people.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to straighten out one or two points, to prevent the discussion in this debate from going too far afield. It has been suggested in the motion that the United States government has put an embargo on coal for shipment to Canada from United States ports. That is not the fact. The fact is that coal has been moving into United States ports in excess of the unloading and yard capacities to handle the cars. The embargo is of a type that is sometimes imposed at the head of the lakes during the grain rush, that is, an embargo against the loading of grain until the congestion at the lakehead could be cleared away. Any boat that can take coal to Canada is being loaded, and coal is moving freely in cars to the extent of the availability of the equipment and the ability of the railroads to move that equipment. I may say that the United States government has always recognized the position of Canada, and is doing so on the present occasion. It is, as it always has been, and is being most helpful in aiding Canada in obtaining her coal requirements.

Coal-Embargo

On several occasions I have sounded a note of alarm with regard to the present position of our coal supply in this country. We entered the summer season with stocks unusually depleted. Canada, owing to the fact that her coal movement must take place in the summer months, has been accustomed to carrying comparatively large stockpiles of coal. The movement of coal was difficult throughout the war, and gradually those stockpiles were reduced until at the beginning of this season of navigation we had very little coal in stock in the country. The movement of coal after the opening has been disappointing. Up to the time of the bituminous coal strike in the United States, the movement had been very much smaller than was usual in any corresponding period in the last few years. The bituminous strike stopped the movement almost wholly. The anthracite coal strike which followed greatly curtailed the movement of domestic coal into this country, and the shipping strike which followed closely on the heels of both has practically brought the movement of coal into this country to a standstill. The result is that we are at least 5,500,000 tons short of the position that we should be in at this season of the year, with no present indication that the situation can be corrected. The fact is that Canada produces 17,000,000 tons of coal and imports 25,000,000 tons, the imports being almost wholly into the central provinces. That coal is imported from the United States.
Much has been said about correcting the situation by mining more Alberta coal, and by shipping more coal from Nova Scotia. The movement of coal from Alberta is limited by the ability of our railroads to move the coal. We have planned for this year a movement of 1,000,000 tons from Alberta to the central provinces, which will be twice the movement that we have ever had in a similar period. That is a phenomenally large movement of Alberta coal to Ontario, and it is all that the railroads believe can possibly be moved. When that coal is moved it will represent one twenty-fifth of the requirements of the two central provinces.
Shipping limitations would make it impossible this year to move more than 3,000,000 tons of coal from Nova Scotia into central Canada. However, we shall be fortunate if we are able to move 1,000,000 tons of coal from the east owing to the fact that production in the maritime provinces provides little surplus over the actual requirements of the maritime provinces. If we could increase the production of coal in the maritime provinces from 5,000,000 tons to 7,000,000 tons, we could

probably ship 3,000,000 tons into the central provinces. But there again, if we are able to do that we would be receiving from the maritime provinces only three twenty-fifths of the requirements of the central provinces.
The cold fact of the matter is that we are dependent for the bulk of our coal supplies in the two central provinces on shipments from the United States, and there is no physical means of replacing that coal from other sources. That is a situation which I have never attempted to minimize. Anyone who interjects any note of optimism into the present fuel situation in Canada is misleading the people of Canada. It is a serious situation. Steps have been taken to increase the supplies of fuel oil, both light oil for domestic purposes and heavy oil for industrial purposes. I am happy to be able to report that some progress has been made in that direction. But there again if the coal equivalent of all the fuel oil that can be brought in and stored in this country, or that can be refined in this country, is added to the movement from eastern and western Canada, it means only a matter of two million additional tons of coal. Once again I say that our position next winter will depend wholly on our ability to move coal from the United States into the two central provinces.
It has been claimed in some sources that Canada has no national fuel policy. As a matter of fact it can be said that since 1928 the government has had a definite national fuel policy. In the years 1928 to 1944 there was paid out as assistance to the movement of Nova Scotia coal to Quebec and Ontario a sum of approximately $25,000,000. During the same period there was paid out for the assistance of the movement of coal from Alberta and eastern British Columbia approximately $10,000,000. In addition, between the years 1931 and 1944 the British Columbia industry received assistance on exports and bunker shipments totalling approximately $1,250,000. Nor is that all. From 1930 to 1945 approximately $3,500,000 was paid to the steel industry of Nova Scotia as a bonus for coal entering into the manufacture of steel, and up to 1944 a further sum of $630,000 was paid out under the Domestic Fuel Act on coal entering into the production of gas and coke. Further encouragement to the Canadian coal industry is provided by a duty of seventy-five cents a ton on bituminous coal and fifty cents a ton on United States anthracite. In short, I say that Canada has had a national fuel policy.
I would point out that it is not practical from a short-range viewpoint, for Canada to become self-sufficient as regards coal. The

Coal-Embargo
present estimated consumption of coal in Ontario and Quebec, practically all from the United States, is around 25,900,000 tons per year. Based upon our experience after the last war ended, considering the immense backlog of orders and requirements for manufactured goods, and the probable necessity of moving large tonnages of grain and other food products for export, it can be expected that our coal requirements in this area will remain over 20,000,000 tons for some years.
With a prospective heavy grain movement from western Canada, the present railway facilities will be pressed to the limit to move east 1,000,000 tons of coal, and this requirement, plus the extra coal needed by t'he railways in the west, will take up practically all available output. From eastern Canada, if production was up to a figure of 7,000.000 tons instead of approximately 5,000,000 tons, it might be possible to move up to 3,000,000 tons. Because of the heavy demand for steel and manufactures of all kinds, it is not practical to consider any substantial increase in railway facilities, since our capacity in that direction will be more or less fully employed in replacing the present equipment that has been worked to capacity during the war. Therefore for some time yet it is simply not practicable to supply our central Canadian coal requirements to any large extent from Canadian sources. The longer range policy is at present under review by the royal commission on coal, and will be examined in the light of the report. An interim report has been requested of the commission, and it is hoped that something will be obtained from that source which will help us in planning a shorter range project. Let me say again, however, that the government cannot change the geography of Canada, nor can it ignore the immutable laws of economics.
The hon. member for Broadview, who introduced this motion, has been for many years an advocate of a national coal policy. I notice that as early as March, 1923, he proposed a resolution in this house demanding that the government institute a national coal policy. I believe that his insistence in advocating such a policy has been a spur to succeeding governments in doing what has been done in that direction. I am only sorry that some steps cannot be taken at this time which will represent an effective short-range policy. But I can assure the hon. member that when the report of the royal commission is received, steps will be taken by the government to see that so serious a situation cannot arise in the future.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to this motion may I make a preliminary observation: I am a little disappointed that the minister rose in his seat just when I did. I am quite happy, of course, to have you, Mr. Speaker, see the minister before you saw me. He has been honoured to-day, and is a much more important gentleman than the hon. member for Macleod. But I might just mention that too often in debates of this kind our Conservative friends are heard, our C.C.F. friends are heard, and then a minister rises as though there were nobody else in the house to be heard. That very often happens.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to make it clear that I must go to a garden party: that is the reason for my rising when I did.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
We shall have a little party here for a while. The minister is not the only one who wants to go to the garden party. It may be that the group in this corner of the house, speaking, as it does, usually with some authority, causes ministers to rise first in order that they may not be embarrassed by having to answer certain questions which we in this corner might put to them.
However, I am glad that the minister did speak, because what he said is to me an apology for a poor case. He sounded an alarm. He has risen on other occasions and sounded an alarm as to the seriousness of the situation, advising the coal dealers to cut down on their sales because there might be a serious shortage before winter. That is not good enough. We in Canada should have no need of these alarms. Then, again, he tried to focus some of the responsibility and cast some of the blame upon the railroads, on the ground that their capacity was limited. We have had railroads in this country for a good many years, and during the war years they were taxed to capacity, but certainly to-day their capacity cannot be more heavily taxed than it was then. To me, therefore, the minister's apology in that respect was a weak one. He goes on to tell us why this emergency exists to-day. Well, what we rise to tell him is why the emergency should not exist to-day. He tried to convince us; in fact his words were definite, that Canada did have, and has had since 1928, a definite fuel policy. If that is so, it must have broken down somewhere; and if his statement is correct I should like to ask him why it was found necessary last year to bring into existence the Carroll coal commission, whose terms of reference were to study the whole problem of the coal industry in Canada and report
Coal-Embargo

back with some definite fuel policy for the future. His argument there, I am afraid, does not hold water.
The present emergency does not directly affect the Macleod constituency, for we have in that area many mines which can well supply our own people. But it affects my constituency to the extent that we have a large coal mining industry there, in the Crowsnest pass, and that industry is well aware that over the years Canada has not had an adequate national fuel policy. Commissions have been set up, and many committees and boards have reviewed from time to time the coal situation in this country. In fact, we have had a Canadian fuel board whose business it is to go into all branches of research and advise the government on the coal problems of the day. In spite of this, we are in a situation where the people of Canada, a country which produces 18 per cent of the world's coal supply, are likely to go cold and industry is likely to have to stop its wheels of production.
When the war broke out I took a particular interest in this matter, for I recognized that if the coal mining industry did not function properly our war industries would be seriously affected. I took the time to write an exhaustive letter to three ministers of the crown, -the then Minister of Labour, the then Minister of Mines and Resources, and the Minister of Munitions and Supply. I explained in my letter to them that the past records of production of coal in the United States, on which we were dependent for our own coal, showed that should there be any disruption in the coal mining industry there, even to a slight extent, it would seriously affect the industrial war effort of Canada. I put before the minister the seriousness of that situation, for this was before the United States came into the war. I visualized the eventuality of strikes taking place in the United States and I wanted him to guard against the results of any such strikes. I tried to persuade him to tackle the problem before such an emergency arose.
What was the result of those three letters? Tire Minister of Mines and Resources-not the present minister, but the hon. gentleman who then occupied the office-did not reply to my letter at all; and since that time he has been politically rewarded, for to-day he sits in another place. I do not believe the Minister of Munitions and Supply answered my letter, but I may have to stand corrected in that regard because I am trusting to my memory. The only minister who replied was the then Minister of Labour, the Hon. Mr. McLarty. He told me that he had submitted my letter to his officials for study and advice.

I spoke to him personally on the matter, again trying to show him the seriousness of possible events. Eventually I received a reply from him to the effect that his advisers had gone into the matter very carefully and had even gone so far as to interview-perhaps it was by way of correspondence, because I do not recall-the officials at Washington, and he stated that they were not overalarmed about the situation. They thought they had everything under control.
It was just fortunate perhaps that events did not turn out adversely during the war; but the war is over now, and have they had everything under complete control? W'e are now faced with an emergency which might have occurred in those days. Fortunately for us it did not, but we are now faced with it, and the government is at a loss to know what to do.
There are one or two other things that have affected the production of coal in Canada in the past and are perhaps still affecting it. One of these is the taxation policy of the government w'ith regard to incomes, because there are man3- coal miners who will not work six days of the week when by working five days their income remains w'ithin certain brackets, whereas by working the extra day-in fact, it is not an extra day but one of the six days in the week-their incomes jump to a higher bracket and, by reason of taxation in that bracket, they work for much less for that extra day. They say, "What is the use? We will stay at home." The coal mines have stayed open just the same. They do not close down altogether because of that extra day, but many manhours have been lost and a great deal of the production of coal has been curtailed. The result is that we have not mined as much coal because of that particular income taxation policy.
Again, there have been times when coal cars have not been available for the transportation of this coal, and it has not always been because these cars were used for some other purpose. Many times they have stood idle on the side tracks.
The government of this day and governments of the past must take the responsibility themselves for this emergency. No one else is to blame in a country of this kind, endowed with rich coal deposits such as Canada has. There is no excuse for such a situation. If the people of Canada go cold-well, they will not be cold to-day while the minister is at the garden party, but if they go cold this winter, then they should know where to place the blame; they will put it there and they will speak in a voice that political parties will hear at the next election.

Coal-Embargo
There is one other matter I wish to bring to the minister's attention. Perhaps it will be considered as not so important, but there has appeared in some of the newspapers recently the suggestion that a good deal of natural gas in Canada could be piped to our eastern cities. I have not gone into the practicability of that suggestion. I think it is a matter of finance, finding the money to do it. I am quite sure the minister will be able to find the suitable expressions to tell us that it is not practicable, but my constituency happens to take in a part, of the Turner valley oil fields. I have wondered many times, as many tourists must wonder, and many honest Canadians must have wondered, at the tremendous waste of natural gas that goes on in those oil fields. There have been da3's when millions of cubic feet of gas simply burned in the air-every day, as someone says. I have been in those parts and have seen huge flares. You could not get within two or three hundred yards of them without being scorched. There they were burning, day in and day out, year in and year out. I sometimes think such waste is not only a tragedy but an insult to omnipotent creative genius; for the kind Creator has put these things in the ground for the use of his creatures, and what happens? We take them and blow them back in his face.

cheap experiment, but one which would turn out to be of great advantage to the Canadian people. It might mean a little disruption in something else; some other industry might be affected by it. Well, governments in power have the responsibility to bring in other legislation so that the whole economy of the country can run smoothly year in and year out. In spite of any praise that can be given to the government for that which they may do-and that applies to all governments-I say to the house that they have miserably failed in respect of a fuel policy for Canada and the Canadian people.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I had originally intended to reply to the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell). But in the course of his speech he told the story of the three letters which he wrote to ministers, the first one to a minister who became a senator, the second one to a minister who did not reply to him and became a right honourable, and the third minister who replied to him and has now passed to the great beyond; consequently I have decided to leave the matter as it is.
The motion contained two points. First of all, it dealt with the embargo, and, second, with the great lakes strike. The minister's words on the embargo warmed the house when he assured us that there was no such thing as an embargo. Then the question about the great lakes strike comes up for consideration. I appreciate that there is a great deal of confusion in the country as to responsibility. To-day's papers carry the story that the government have laid down a formula which has been accepted by the seamen but has been rejected by the operators. My hon. friend said that the blame ought to be placed where it belongs. All I say is that the house ought to point at the people who are to blame for not settling the strike, and it certainly is not the seamen's union.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words in connection with this matter. There is no doubt that we are confronted with a grave emergency so far as the coal situation is concerned. As the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) said, it is not something that has developed overnight, and it has not developed because of any one particular circumstance. Undoubtedly what has intensified the situation is the strike on the great lakes. If that
Coal-Embargo

strike should be settled quickfy, perhaps some of the urgency of the crisis would be overcome, but it would not be overcome entirely.
There is a general shortage of coal to-day, pretty well all over the world, and Canada cannot fail to be affected by that to some extent. It is not solely a matter of providing the necessary money. Some mention was made of the fact that $30 million would be required to do certain work in connection with taking natural gas from Alberta and bringing it to Toronto. Perhaps the $30 million could be found much easier for that kind of work than the material and the labour. What the world is confronted with to-day is not that we cannot find the money to do these things. It has been demonstrated that we can find the money. The difficulty which faces us now is that of finding the material and labour, and finding the material is largely a matter of finding the labour to produce the material. It is a matter of organization.
The providing of the necessities of life- and this is one other proof that the providing of the necessities of life can no longer be left to the vagaries of private enterprise which may or may not do the things required [DOT]-is of paramount importance.
The failure in the coalfields began shortly after the last war. The failure of the coalfields to meet satisfactorily the requirements of people in the various parts of the world began after the last war and it has developed progressively ever since. It is a matter of coal competing with another and cheaper fuel, namely electricity. What the government should do now, regardless of how soon the seamen's strike is settled, is to formulate a national coal policy so that this country can make the best of its great natural resources in western and eastern Canada.
I happened to be in Halifax in October, 1938. There I met a delegation which came from the village of Thorburn, Nova Scotia, to meet the government when the proprietors of the coal mine there, the Dominion Steel and Coal company, I assume, had decided to close that mine. By that action they not only deprived the country of a certain amount of fuel but completely deprived the fifteen hundred or so people of that village-I believe there were some three hundred men working in the mine-of their only means of subsistence. This delegation pointed out that while the existing mine was about depleted of its coal, right within that very district there was an enormous amount of the best coal in Nova Scotia which could be developed; but the owners of the mine said they were not going to develop it until times were more propitious

for that to be done. So I repeat that the people of Canada are not going to overcome these difficulties until the government, on behalf of the people, will organize a national fuel policy in order to make available to ourselves the fuel, coal and other fuels, with which this country is so richly endowed.
All I would say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, is that of course we should adopt every means possible to settle the seamen's strike quickly. Since the eight-hour day is the root cause of the trouble, it is up to the government to see that the eight-hour day is put into effect on all Canadian ships. That would be the first step in ending this emergency. The next step, as I said, is the creation of a long-term national fuel policy which will make use of all our fuel resources.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before I proceed with what I had intended to say, might I refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) who has just taken his seat. The hon. member never misses an opportunity of casting a slur against private enterprise. He pretends to argue that if only the mines of Canada were in the hands of the government there would be no difficulty with respect to this coal situation. Once more the bon. member completely misses the point. Even if the government owned every mine in Alberta and every mine in Nova Scotia, if the government were not prepared to subsidize the transportation of that coal into Ontario and Quebec and to adopt other policies which would result in the distribution of Canadian coal throughout Canada, then certainly the government would have no solution of the problem and we would be in exactly the position in which we are now.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman allow me a word, since he has brought my mind into his argument? I think he is the one who is missing the point. I would assume that if the government organized a coal policy for the people of Canada, they would do that very thing.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: If the hon. member had only said that, instead of continuing his incessant slur against private enterprise, he might get somewhere.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I did not cast any slurs against private enterprise.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: We shall let Hansard decide.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: My hon. friend can come to their assistance if he wishes.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
My hon. friend and I will settle this some time in the future. Just

Coal-Embargo
now we are talking about a coal policy, and the important thing is to keep one's eye on the ball. In this case the ball is to get all the coal needful in Canada mined and distributed to Canadians. Government ownership or private ownership of the mines makes not the slightest difference; there are other matters involved.
A national coal policy for Canada has been neglected up to the present time, as has been pointed out by several hon. members who have already spoken; and because of that neglect we are now facing this dangerous situation. Why has a national fuel policy been neglected? When I first came to Ottawa in 1936 and began to have some contact with ministers of the crown I tried to urge upon those who were then in power the necessity of developing a national fuel policy, for very much the same reasons which were advanced by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell). But I found nothing but deaf ears, which quite confounded me. There were thousands and thousands of unemployed in the mining areas of Alberta. The railroads lacked freight to haul. There was every reason that could be conceived why we should develop our coal industry and bring Canadian coal into Ontario and Quebec. Yet I found no interest; or if there was interest there was only a sort of indulgent and helpless shrug of the shoulders and hands, which quite astonished me. I wondered why, and I have wondered ever since. I have wondered if it is because a great deal of Canadian money is invested in certain mining concerns in the United States, and if certain Canadian interests wanted to have the coal from those mines brought into Canada to find a market here. I have never been able to have that question answered to my own satisfaction, but I have heard rumours which would indicate that the thought was perhaps not entirely without justification.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext: It is not a slur on private enterprise; it is an instance of mismanagement on the part of the government. Of course private enterprise needs to be taken care of, just the same as any ordinary man driving on the street has to be taken care of. A man driving an automobile has to be taken care of by wise traffic regulations; otherwise he may get into trouble. So we introduce and support regulations to see that an automobile drive does not injure people. Why cannot hon. members of the C.C.F. think straight? How is it they are forever short-circuiting their intelligence like that?

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Some of these days there will be a real free for all between myself and the C.C.F. I will take them all on, if I can get them one at a time. I will gladly take them on one at a time, on this question, at any time, because they are just all wrong in their thinking.
There has been a definite neglect on the part of Ontario and Quebec. It is all very well for hon. members from Ontario to rise now and complain about the shortage of fuel in that province. I deeply sympathize with them. But, Mr. Speaker, Ontario and Quebec have been in charge of the policies of Canada for fifty years now; and if those policies have not resulted in a sane development of our Canadian coal resources, then the hon. members from Ontario and Quebec have no one but themselves to blame. It is quite certain that the people of Nova Scotia and the people of Alberta have been eager to develop a national coal policy at least ever since confederation.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I might say that during my first term in this house I advocated a national coal policy.

maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I quite appreciate that there have been some men of vision like the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) and the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), but I must say I have heard no other hon. member of the Progressive Conservative party advocate a national fuel policy until the present time. On other occasions I have heard hon. members from the maritimes rise and plead for a national coal policy, and I have seen hon. members from Ontario and Quebec leave the chamber and refuse to listen to them. They are now going to suffer for their misdeeds. So let us not entirely blame the government, because, after all, governments are controlled by the people who elect the members who support the government; and the people who elect the members who support and control this government are the people of Ontario and Quebec. Let that be thoroughly impressed upon the minds of the people of Ontario and Quebec in all their anxiety about fuel. The solution is in their own hands.
One of the main reasons why governments in Ottawa have not adopted a national fuel policy has been that for some reason or another those governments have rigidly refused to consider a policy of national self-sufficiency. We see that with respect to every commodity that might be named. I -have faced it for years in connection with the sugar question. One cannot rise in this house and advocate a
Coal-Embargo

national sugar policy for Canada, but immediately the answer is that we must have trade. I suppose the reason we have not had a national fuel policy for Canada is that we must have trade, even if w'e 'have to bring in coal from the United States and run divers dangerous risks in order to have that trade. There has been danger, and there is danger to-day of a serious adverse trade balance between Canada and the United States, a balance against Canada. Every well informed person knows that. Notwithstanding that fact, we have persisted in importing millions and millions of tons of coal from the United States, thereb}'' aggravating the adverse trade balance, instead of developing the coal industry in this country. How can that possibly be excused?
It has been clear to every man charged with responsibility for the last twenty years that there was the greatest kind of danger of an economic struggle in the United States which would tie up production there, and render us vulnerable in the matter of a fuel supply, exactly as has happened to-day. How is it that there has been such a complete lack of vision on the part of those in control of the policies of this country ? It will not be so serious if we can have repentance now.
I speak as a representative from one of the major coal producing areas in Alberta. I say that when coal has been shipped from my province to Ontario, our coal, according to reports reaching me, has been mixed in Ontario with trash, with fine pulverized material, literally muck in some cases, and has been delivered as Alberta coal. The object was purely that of discrediting Alberta coal in the minds of the people in Ontario and Quebec, and especially those in Ontario. Nefarious practices such as that are beyond any possibility of condonement. Those things have happened.
Then, we have seen United States producers dumping coal, with apparently nothing being done about it. I am informed that coal producers in the United States have adopted a policy under which they have sold the coal necessary to supply their own needs, and to give them a profit. Then they have had available a vast quantity of coal to be dumped in Canada at almost any price. That coal has been dumped here, while the government has supinely allowed that to take place, notwithstanding the danger involved so far as Alberta and Nova Scotia producers were concerned.
I am informed that as a result of these dumping practices coal from United States coal fields has been delivered at Winnipeg, a city which unquestionably should be a market for Alberta coal. But that whole process has been allowed to proceed.
[Mr. Blackmore.J
Let me repeat that there is only one group of people in Canada to blame for all this, and those are the people in Ontario and Quebec. While the people in Ontario and Quebec have been buying their coal from United States mines, Alberta coal miners by the thousands have been working only two or three days a week, and Alberta coal producing areas have become distress areas, with resultant bad fortune to Ontario producers of goods. How can that possibly be justified? This sort of thing must change in the future if we are ever to be independent of such mishaps as those from which we are now suffering.
There has been too much of determination on the part of people at Ottawa to look at money rather than goods. They have refused to grant adequate subsidies. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) spoke about a national fuel policy in 1928. What was the matter with that national fuel policy of 1928, and thereafter? It was the simple fact that they would not grant large enough subsidies to make sure that coal from Alberta could be put on the Ontario market in a position to compete with the United States product. At any time they could have increased the subsidy so as to have allowed Alberta to sell her coal in Ontario in any quantities desired. That would have resulted in a fuel policy which would have rendered us more or less self-sufficient, and invulnerable to such mishaps as now confront us.
What has been the real situation with regard to Alberta? We in Alberta have, according to our estimates, 14 per cent of the world's total supply of coal. We have 21 per cent of the coal on the north American continent, We have 72 per cent of the coal in the British empire, and 87 per cent of that in Canada. It is estimated by one authority that in Alberta we have 40,200 million tons of coal, consisting of four different types, namely lignite, sub-bituminous, bituminous and semianthracite. Surely, from all those different kinds of coal any ordinary needs of consumers in Ontario and Quebec could have been supplied.
The question arises: What are we to do with this situation? After all, there is no use in recrimination. Now that we are in this time of grave danger, let us look to the future and devise, if possible, some solution of the problem. I must agree with the minister in large measure when he says that a real immediate solution of the problem looks uncertain at the present time. At least, however, we can perform a right-about-face in the matter of fuel policy and resolve that as soon as we have an opportunity, we are going to do something sound about it.

Coal-Embargo
Let the government firmly declare to-day -and I ask hon. members from Ontario and Quebec to listen to this, and see how they agree with this procedure-that it will have a national self-sufficient policy with respect to fuel. How many members from Ontario and Quebec would support the government 100 per cent if it indicated its stern resolve and intention that from this day forward it would have a national fuel policy under which we would use coal produced in Canada? That is the test. If hon. members from Ontario and Quebec would not support the government in an all-out policy of that kind, then they must themselves to-day accept blame for the fact that no sound foundation has been laid for a future fuel policy in Canada, and no real commencement made with respect to providing fuel immediately.
The next question is: Would hon. members from Ontario and Quebec support the government if to-morrow it announced a policy under which it would subsidize Alberta and Nova Scotia coal to the extent that they would penetrate the markets of Ontario and Quebec, and to the extent that they would fill the requirements of those markets? JI wonder how many members from those two provinces would support the government in such a policy.

Well, we have seen one hon. member rise in his place; do I see others? That is the test. As a matter of fact, we people in Canada must have a change in our outlook. We must make up our minds individually, so far as it is possible, that we are going to have a policy of national selfsufficiency, that we are going to produce those things we need, produce them in our own country, and not import them from abroad, or from sources upon which we cannot depend. Until wre do that we shall always be in danger of a situation such as that now facing us.
Then, I wonder if the Ontario and Quebec members would support the government in the establishment of plants in which could be processed Alberta and Nova Scotia coals, 63260-156
bringing the products of those processes into the Ontario and Quebec markets. By that I mean this: Just as the Germans during the last war, and before it, produced a high percentage of their gasoline and oil from coal deposits in that country, so we in Canada could produce our gasoline and oil from coal deposits in Alberta and Nova Scotia.
The question is, would the Ontario and Quebec members support the government if it were to bring in a policy of that-kind? It would be the solution of some problems for the future. Suppose the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply were to rise in his place to-morrow and say to hon. members, "This government has become convinced, because of the crisis facing us, that its policy in the past has been wrong, and from this time forward the government guarantees all members of the house that if hon. members will give their support it will bring in a national fuel policy under which it will subsidize coal from Alberta, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and other points, to the extent that those coals will supply the market in Canada, and it will subsidize far enough to make sure that they do, and the government will protect the markets in Canada against dumping by the United States or any other place by such measures as may be found appropriate and adequate. The question is: If the minister were to say that, would the members of this house support the government in so doing? Let the minister further declare: The government will institute a pollicy of processing the coal in various parts of Canada in order to obtain the gasoline and other oils that we need in this country and thus make the country independent of' any outside source."
If the government would rise and do that, do you know what would happen all over Alberta? Private enterprise, which the hon. member for Vancouver East so much deprecates, would immediately take steps to open new mines, to put in new equipment and to train personnel. The railroads would immediately buy rolling stock and lay tracks so that the coal could be delivered in Ontario and Quebec. There would be a market guaranteed and a price guaranteed. We would then be on a way to a solution of the problem. We could perhaps not possibly overtake the unfortunate shortages which have developed, but we could certainly greatly improve conditions as they now are.
There are in Alberta rich mines capable of vast production which are not producing coal to-day. Why? Because it would cost too much to build railroad lines into them or to do certain other things Private enterprise

Coal-Embargo

does not dare to go in and spend the money, because probably by next year there would be no Canadian fuel difficulty and all the equipment that had been put in would be left idle. If the government put in the equipment right away now, then we would have the members of the Progressive Conservative party next year painting the air in this chamber blue because the government had wasted a lot of money on the projects.
There is only one thing to do. We should uake up our minds that we are going to aecome nationally self-sufficient. We must make up our minds that we are going to have an adequate fuel policy, no matter what it costs. We should go to work on that policy. Then we should find that private enterprise would be doing its part. There would be no need of any government enterprise as far as coal is concerned. A great deal of improvement in our situation could be brought about even between now and Christmas, or February.
Let me repeat that the great question is: Are Ontario and Quebec repentant? Are they ready to break new sod? Are they ready to blaze a new trail with respect to a fuel policy in this country? Is this house ready to make new resolutions with respect to a fuel policy? If not, then I must say that we shall just go on in the dangerous way we have been going these many years. I see no other way in the world out of our difficulty.
Before I resume my seat, I should like to refer for a moment or two to the matter of gas wastage which was brought up by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell). The hon. member was referring more to the condition which had obtained in the Turner valley before' the Social Credit government took charge in Alberta. At that time there was immense wastage of gas in the Turner valley; there were flares burning all the time. But the Alberta Social Credit government, by its introduction of a wise conservation policy with respect to gas, has reduced the number of those flares to two small ones. In the past four years there has been a laudable curtailment of the waste. Gas which was formerly allowed to escape has been conducted back into the chambers within the earth, so that it will help force the gasoline up through the wells. The whole process is called repressurizing.
Because of this policy there is not nearly as much waste as once occurred. However, the argument advanced by the hon. member for Macleod still holds good. There is in Alberta a tremendous amount of natural gas that could be brought into this part of the country if pipes were laid and a market

guaranteed. We could process the coal in Alberta so that we should have gasoline and other kinds of oil that could be piped to any other part of Canada to supply the needs for these products just as long as those needs exist. All that is necessary is to guarantee a certain market and a suitable price. Then private enterprise will know that when it invests its money it is not going to lose it. If the government invests money the government will not then be accused by some excited opposition of having wasted the country's money. I leave this discussion for the time being at that stage.

Mr. Speaker, I come from Cumberland which contains the second largest coal fields in eastern Canada. Our people are interested in the Canadian coal requirements. I have been associated with those who have advocated a national coal and steel policy for many years. The leader of that movement was the late Hon. Gordon S. Harrington, who was minister of mines and minister of labour of Nova Scotia. He advocated this policy in 1925, and from then on, with some success. The result was that a million and a half tons of coal were shipped per year from Nova Scotia into central Canada which had never been shipped before. The people were educated to the use of our coal and they soon began to appreciate its qualities.
There was an oversupply of productive capacity in Nova Scotia and a limited local market. Mines vrere operating only one, two or three days a week and there was an uncertain market for what was produced. Our coal came into competition with cheap coal which was brought from overseas as bunker coal and with coal imported from the United States. At that time we were told that coal was being produced in coal fields in Ohio which had been owned by the Grand Trunk railway and taken over by the Canadian National Railways for ninety-one cents a ton, and later as low as eighty-nine cents a ton.
It was difficult to put this Canadian fuel policy into effect. It was necessary to increase the duty on coal and to pay subventions which were largely paid for by the duty. I was disappointed at hearing the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) state that the production in Nova Scotia is only
5,500,000	tons for the current year; this in the face of a great need for coal.
The production in Nova Scotia was a minimum of 7,000,000 tons, with the expectation of an increase to 9,000,000 or 10,000,000 tons per year. On two or three occasions I have asked
.TUNE 13, 1946
Questions
the minister what efforts were being made to canvass the Situation in Nova Scotia to get greater production. I asked him if the miners and operators were being consulted to obtain more coal to supply the needs of Ontario and Quebec.
One reason for the reduced production in Nova Scotia is that many miners entered the armed forces early in the war. Those were trained miners who were capable of the greatest production. Unfortunately some of them were killed; many were wounded, and some are not willing to go back into the mines. However, I think much could be done to increase production in Nova Scotia if all concerned were approached in the right way. We are fortunate in having a capable royal commission studying the coal question under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice Carroll and we are waiting patiently for their report. I am hopeful that when their report is presented to parliament a coal and fuel policy will be agreed on that will not only prove beneficial to the producing areas but will make central Canada more secure in obtaining the utmost supply of Canadian coal.
Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview); I rise to close the debate. I admit under the rules I have no right to say any more, but I should like two or three minutes to do so. This doctrine of a national fuel supply has been Conservative doctrine since I first introduced it on March 19, 1923. Ontario and Quebec have no coal.
