subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Nor do I. My time has practically expired. I do not intend to speak much longer to-night. As a matter of fact, I did not intend to speak as long as I have done, but I felt impelled to speak on behalf of the maritime provinces, and especially the province from which I come.
I should like to give a short quotation used in the speech delivered by the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. Hazen), as reported at page 2268 of Hansard of June 6: He quoted section 52 of the British North America Act to emphasize the point which he made. Section 52 reads:
The number of members of the House of Commons may be from time to time increased by the parliament of Canada, provided the proportionate representation of the provinces prescribed by this act is not thereby disturbed.
We of New Brunswick have ten members out of 245 in the House of Commons. If this amendment is passed we shall have ten members out of 255 and, as the hon. member for St. John-Albert said the other day this section of the British North America Act will be violated because the proportionate representation of New Brunswick will be greatly disturbed. As I say, we have ten out of 245. Ten out of 255 is not the same proportion, and any hon. member who will take the time to consider it will see that that is a fact.
I wish to make this further statement. Last night one hon. member suggested that because I was speaking for my own province I was not a good Canadian. I have sat in this house and listened to practically every hon. member from Quebec who has spoken, and each has spoken almost entirely on the effect that this amendment would have on that province. I and no other member would suggest that, on that account, he was not a good Canadian. The same is true of hon. members from western Canada. They have all considered this matter almost entirely from the point of view of their own section of the country, and I contend that when I debate this question as it affects New Brunswick I am no less a Canadian than are those members from Quebec or from any other part of Canada.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: In rising to take part in this debate, I quite realize that what I have to say will not be popular on this side of the house.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Do not worry.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I wish to make it clear at the outset that I intend to vote against the resolution introduced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent). Following the remarks made by the speaker who has just taken his seat, let me make it clear that I am going to deal with the matter from the point of view of British Columbia, and I do not want any taunt hurled at me that I am not thinking as a Canadian. Let us be frank. There is not a man sitting in this house but must and does think provincially. Every hon. member here is thinking of his own constituency and of his own province. Why have accusations hurled across the floor that those who do are not Canadians? The man who does not think of this resolution in terms
Redistribution

of his own province is somewhat derelict in his duty. He is no less a Canadian if he thinks of it in terms of his own province.
I listened with a great deal of attention to the remarks of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), and the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett). Although I am not a lawyer, I think they entirely missed the point of the resolution, and I shall tell the house why. If one looks over the British North America Act he will see that there are certain sections dealing with general clauses and powers given to the dominion. Then there are certain powers specifically defined as powers of the dominion and of the provincial governments. It is my opinion as a layman that if the dominion government were interfering or asking the British parliament to amend any of the sections under which the provincial governments have power they would then have, first of all, to go to the provinces and ask for the right to do so. But under the general clauses dealing with redistribution it is my opinion that the dominion government has the power to bring in this resolution without consulting the provinces. However, I shall say that when the British government read the resolution in its present form they will be in just as much doubt as the members of the house were when it was first introduced, because I doubt whether many hon. members would have understood the resolution had it not been for the explanation given by the Minister of Justice. In my opinion it is extremely clumsily worded and in fact somewhat misleading because it says:
And whereas it is considered that a more equitable apportionment of members to the various provinces could be effected if readjustment were made on the basis of the population of all the provinces taken as a whole.
We are not doing that, I think it is explained in the last two clauses that we are not taking the population of the provinces as a whole, because when we come to divide by 250 we leave out Prince Edward Island, the northwest territories and the Yukon. Therefore the wording of the resolution is certainly misleading in the beginning, and it is not until you get to the end of the resolution that you find the meat of it. I was not at all surprised that the Minister of Justice, when asked by an hon. member how he arrived at the figure 250, should reply, "Well, I don't know\" I doubt if many hon. members could say how that figure was arrived at as a quotient; but I say it was a clever piece of mathematics, whoever was responsible for it.
Before I pass on to some figures and further statements, may I say that in the amendment I believe the hon. member for Lake Centre, if
fMr. Rekt.l
he spoke for his party, inadvertently or otherwise has tied up his party with the principle of the Canadian government going to the British parliament for amendments to the British North America Act. Probably he did not intend to do that, but that is the actual effect of the amendment. Of course I for one believe that this Canada should have the right to amend its own constitution without going to the British parliament.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the leader of the C.C.F. party, spoke in favour of the resolution, and I am not altogether surprised at that, since Saskatchewan stands to gain under it. He and every other leader know the troubles that arise when you have to reduce the representation of a province. The hon. gentleman comes to this house with a large number of members from Saskatchewan, and I can visualize his difficulties if he should be told that there would be four less constituencies, for he then would have to say to the members of his party, "Well, which of you boys are going to stay home?"

All of them, I hope.
Mr. R.EID:	Then last evening the hon.
member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) gave his views as to what that party would do in regard to the senate, should they come to power. May I say to him and to the leader of the C.C.F., after having looked into the number of members, that if this resolution passes the house and the increased numbers are given the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, the C.C.F. will wait an additional twenty-five years before they take over the reins of government; and I say that in all sincerity.
In regard to the increased representation for the province of Quebec, I think under the present set-up that province has a real grievance. It has been known for years that Ontario has had seven or eight members too many, according to population. Rather than reduce the number of members from Ontario, however, after someone found out how this new proposal would work, * they come along and add one member to Ontario and eight to Quebec. In all kindliness, I want to tell hon. members from Quebec that if they look over the figures they will see that most of the eight members to be added to the representation of that province are likely to go to the city of Montreal and not to the great hinterland outside. Coming back to what I said a moment ago, however, to my way of thinking this resolution has been introduced at this time to, shall I say, placate Quebec because Ontario has had seven members more than it

should, and to help out the other provinces, especially Saskatchewan, which otherwise would lose four members.
The leader of the C.C.F. party spoke about representation by population. I wonder if he has studied the situation in Canada to-day, if he has looked at the great shift of population which has taken place, at the great number of people who have left Saskatchewan, particularly, and who have gone principally to British Columbia. I know one cannot always judge by the number of electors in speaking of representation by population, but if one looks over the figures for the last election he will find that on the voters' lists of the province of Saskatchewan they had only 445,601 names, with twenty-one members in this house, while we in the province of British Columbia had 545,077 names on the voters' lists and only sixteen members. In other words, we had five members fewer than Saskatchewan, although they had 99,000 fewer on their voters' lists.

But the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who represents that riding, had nothing to do with the number of people in it. I remember one gentleman who has since gone to his reward coming into
this house with the redistribution map and poking his cane right through it; he was so wild. Many hon. members will remember that. Take it or lump it." If anyone cares to look over those maps he will be reminded of one of those cross-word puzzles. subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: The house will be pleased that the cat has got out of the bag at last. I was on that committee, and I do not want to go on one again, because it was just one of those terrible headaches.

speechtext: Would the hon. member favour the setting up of a judicial commission, independent of the house.

I am not convinced that a judicial commission would be the solution. But one thing I am convinced of is that we should

be careful about representation in the house; I believe we are overgoverned. I will give an example. I looked up some figures in regard to Great Britain and in regard to some other countries. In Great Britain the unit is 70.000. I know somebody will say that that is only a small country. But let us take the figures in some old country cities. Let us first take the city of Glasgow.

The Minister of Agriculture asks how many councillors they have. Well, how many councils have we, and how many provincial legislatures have we? We have well over 500 provincial members of legislatures, and councillors in every municipality from Halifax to Vancouver island.
I was about to answer the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. The city of Glasgow has fifteen members. The population of that city at the 1939 census, the last one, was 1,280,473. The nearest comparison I can find in Canada is Montreal with its sixteen members and a population given officially as something over 903.000.

Montreal.

Then, turning to Toronto-and I suppose the Toronto members are waiting to hear what I have to say about that city-I find that Liverpool with a population of 865,688 has eleven members. Toronto has eleven members for 667,491 of population, or a difference of 198,197. I mention this particularly because both the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and I came from the British isles. In his speech he made considerable reference to representation by population. The thought came to my mind: Were they not as well represented there, in the cities in Great Britain, as we are in this country?
However, let us come nearer home, to the United States. What do we find there? We find that they have 435 in their house of representatives, with a unit of 304,000. Will any hon. member say that representation in Washington is not as good for the people of the United States as is our representation in this country? I do not think so.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: How do the countries compare in size?

speechtext: Well, so far as area is concerned, I think Canada is just about the same size as the United States. In fact, I believe it is a little larger. I do not see any point in asking that question. If the hon. member is talking about population, he might have something on that point.

speechtext:
What about the shift in population? What about the situation to-day? We have at the present time in British Columbia
949,000	people. We have had an increase during the war to the extent of 90,000. In fact, only three provinces have had increases in population, increases from one province to another. Those three are Nova Scotia which, according to the official document I have, had an increase of 8,000 in three or four years; Ontario, with an increase of 58,000, and British Columbia with one of 90,000.
Saskatchewan has been gradually losing its population from 1935. It is estimated that in the past three or four years they have lost something like 97,000. Are we going to take any note of those serious changes in population throughout the country? Are we, shall I say, from British Columbia, with a population of 949,000, going to be content with eighteen members, under the new proposal, as compared with a lesser population in Sas-

Redistribution
katchewan, and their being granted twenty members? Surely there is nothing fair about that, when one considers the matter in the light of the great shift in population which has taken place.
I would have had the temerity to move an amendment; but I understand that such would have been a negative motion, and therefore not in order. As I have said, however, I intend to vote against the resolution for the particular reasons I have outlined. I am going to suggest to the government that they take into consideration deferring this matter until after the next census.
Every member in the House of Commons is sitting here as a result of the census figures of 1941.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: It is 1931.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
But have there been any complaints? There have been no complaints from members, at all. Why take hold of the British North America Act and cause all the suspicion, and unrest, shall I say, that we are doing something wrong?
I want to say this to the Minister of Justice, that while it is true from a legal point of view, as he will argue-and I will agree with him-that we have the right to go to the British parliament without consulting the provinces, yet in this particular matter-not in other matters, but we have in this particular one-citizens will look upon the request by this government to Great Britain as something that should be made when we consider further social legislation.
I have just looked at a paper which came from the coast, and I find that the editor of the Vancouver Sun, thinking along the same lines, namely, with respect to by-passing the provinces in this redistribution proposal, has this to say:
It would seem on the face of it that this is purely a federal concern, since it affects only the matter of popular representation in the federal parliament. Yet the precedent is of the greatest importance. If Ottawa can establish the principle that a petition from the dominion parliament alone is necessary to win amendment of the British North America Act, then the principle holds good in every matter affecting the jurisdiction of the provinces and dominion.
Some will argue that the editor of the Vancouver Sun is wrong, and I would argue that legally he may be wrong because there are certain sections of the British North America Act-I am not going to delay the house by reading them-in which the powers of the provinces are specifically defined. Most people, when they see that this government is going to London to ask for an amendment to the British North America Act, will ask,
"What for?" They will be wondering why this is being done when they are told in connection with social legislation that the British North America Act prevents certain things from being done unless the consent of the provinces is first obtained.
I am afraid the average citizen-even more than the average citizen, because here we have the editor of the Vancouver Sun taking the same view and asking the same question- will feel that this action does more harm than the expediency which would seem to have prompted it, that is, the fear of having to reduce the representation of certain provinces to what it should be according to actual population.
I am going to plead with the government to defer taking this action until the next census has been taken. This parliament could go on until 1948 or 1949, at which time it would be within a year or a year and a half of the next decennial census, and it would be much fairer if we were to wait until that took place. If we proceed with the present proposal I am afraid that the high sounding phrases which have been uttered during this debate about representation by population will not carry a great deal of weight.
I realize that I am one of the few on this side of the house who is opposing this proposal. I do it conscientiously because I feel that what is being done is not a proper and correct thing to do at this time. I felt it was my duty to rise and state exactly where I stand on the matter.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few words will enable me to express my views on the matter under discussion. It would be useless for me to deliver a lengthy speech on a measure which meets an obvious need and in favour of which some fellow-members who are well versed in constitutional law have put forward learned opinions. Besides, it is not my habit to deliver long speeches; this session has already been going for such a long time that I would not wish to delay it further.
When the right hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) moved in 1943 the postponement of redistribution until the end of the war, I was one of the nine members who took exception to the proposal. I opposed it because it was a departure from the constitution which provides that the redistribution of constituencies must be proceeded with after each decennial census; I opposed it because in the event of an election being called before the end of the war, the government would have enabled seven or eight members to sit in the House of Commons in violation of the
Redistribution

constitution, while Quebec, even with a material increase in its population, had the same number of representatives. I made the following remarks on July 5, 1943:
Do you not believe, Mr. Speaker, that an injustice is being done as regards the rights which the province of Quebec enjoys under the confederation agreement, and that, under the pretext of war the democratic character of our parliamentary system is being set aside? In my opinion, to postpone the redistribution is simply to check the influence which Quebec is entitled to have on the political destinies of this country.
I went on:
I am opposed to this resolution for the reasons which I have just stated. I consider that I have no right to take any other stand; a principle is involved, and it is also a matter of justice for my province. Besides, this resolution interferes with the constitution, and my province is especially affected. The government has no justification for overriding the constitution.
Redistribution was postponed; the reason advanced was that we were at war. I thought at that time that such a reason was unconvincing and I still think so, since the redistribution bill affected neither directly nor indirectly our war effort, but was purely and simply a matter of administration.
As regards the proposal that is now before the house, it has my unqualified approval. My first reason for supporting it is that it does justice to my province. The British North America Act, passed in 1867, was perhaps equitable at that time; the fathers of confederation certainly acted in accordance with the circumstances and with due regard of what were then the best interests of the people. However, time has shown that the British North America Act has not given the expected results. For instance, was it believed in 1867 that the province of Quebec would take such an expansion, as regards population, and that seventy-five years later the constitution would cause an injustice toward Quebec, whose population has increased almost threefold since 1871.
The British North America Act sets at 65 the number of Quebec representatives. With a population exceeding that of Quebec by
450,000	only the province of Ontario now has 82 members, 17 more than Quebec. The new plan will give Ontario one additional member, or a total of 83; Quebec will have eight more members, or a total of 73. The balance will be restored and I for one am quite glad of it.
Under the present rules, Quebec, with a number of representatives permanently fixed at 65, is the province whose population determines the representation of other provinces. The continuation of the present system would

mean a marked decrease in the number of dominion members, which is inconsistent in view of the expansion achieved by Canada during the last twenty years. The new plan gives to the provinces a representation based on their respective population, and that is a matter of fair play for all of them.
The Progressive Conservatives are opposed to the resolution on the ground that the rights of the provinces are infringed upon and that the provinces should have been consulted. They go so far as to move an amendment along those lines. The prime minister of Quebec, Mr. Duplessis, was the first to expound that argument in a statement he made some time ago. The Conservatives have taken up the argument, which shows the true feelings of the prime minister of my province, to whom the autonomous mantle affords a poor disguise. The Conservatives, in taking up the argument, do not bare their whole thought. The true reason of their opposition lies simply in the fact that the proposal will give eight additional seats to the province of Quebec. And eight additional seats which will never be theirs because the Conservative party, which has barely kept alive in Quebec since 1920, cannot take a new lease on life unless it discards that fanaticism which is so obnoxious to my province and so much at variance with its typical traditions. That fanaticism is well known. We have had fresh evidence of it, and the electors of Quebec will not forget it.
It is suggested that the provinces be consulted. But why should they be? Learned jurists have established in this house that the central government could legislate in the matter now under discussion without consulting the provinces. Besides, it is plain common sense that if a province may change its own representation without permission from the central government, why should the latter seek provincial consent in order to modify its own? Consultation of the provinces would merely kill the plan. It is well known that certain provincial prime ministers are systematically antagonistic to this government, as was strikingly shown at the last dominion-provincial conference. How could Mr. Drew, for instance, agree to the plan when his friends in this house are dead against it? Could Mr. Duplessis favour it when he was frankly opposing it even before it was brought up in this house? The plan would then be set aside just to please some petty politician and Quebec would lose, in parliament, eight additional units of influence on the destinies of this country. We, federal members, are just as ardent advocates of autonomy as Mr. Duplessis, but with a

Redistribution
broader outlook. True autonomy also consists in minding one's own business. We, Quebec members, have been elected to represent the province of Quebec in this parliament; and it is for us, Quebec federal members to say whether or not the province of Quebec is entitled to have eight additional members in the next elections. Such are my full views in the matter.
I favour the resolution. It redresses an injustice toward the province of Quebec. It recognizes Quebec's development and importance. It grants it, in proportion to its population, the number of representatives to which it is entitled. The only feature I dislike is that we should have to apply to London for permission to make changes in our constitution. This is said to be a mere formality. But it is nonetheless quite annoying. I understand that we can, at any time, eliminate this formality merely by a vote. This we should do without delay. There remains no reason why, as a nation, Canada should seek authorizations overseas. I therefore hope that before long-and the sooner the better-parliament will rid itself of this ridiculous obligation.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I first wish to compliment the hon. member for New' Westminster (Mr. Reid) on the address he gave to-night. I believe he has approached this question in the right way. When confederation was first enacted it was viewed, not from the point of view of political expediency, as he said this resolution is, but in a spirit of statesmanship by leaders of both the parties in the different provinces.
I have no written manuscript to-night, but I consider it to be my duty to voice what should be, and I believe are, the views of the electors in Nova Scotia. Someone has the right and the duty to speak for Nova Scotia and, as my seat-mate the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) has said, I do not consider that I am any less a Canadian because I do so.
Nova Scotia has special claims to sympathetic consideration as regards her standing in confederation. Nova Scotia has contributed much in relation to the benefits she has received. There have been disappointments; there is dissatisfaction, and if this resolution is carried and put into effect it is going to accentuate the present discontent in our province. I feel that Nova Scotia should be consulted, and they will not be satisfied unless they are.
When confederation was enacted it was approved by the leaders of both the great parties, but there have been public men in Nova Scotia
who have made it a political issue from that day to this, and thereby profited politically. They ran elections on the cry of repeal. They ran elections in Nova Scotia on the discontent as to its relations with the rest of Canada. To this day hardly a week passes but in my province representations are made against confederation and our relation to the rest of Canada. The point I wish to make is that, if that party was opposed to confederation, if they made a political issue of it for almost eighty years, they will support the hon. member for New Westminster and others, and will surely require that the electors, or the legislature, or the government, or the Premier of Nova Scotia shall be consulted. This has been made a political issue from the day of confederation to the present time. The party with which I am associated has suffered. Not long ago I heard the former premier of Nova Scotia, Hon. A. S. MacMillan, say that he would be favourable to erecting a monument in Nova Scotia to that great Nova Scotian, Sir Charles Tupper, not because of what he did for Nova Scotia and Canada in seeing that confederation was enacted, but because of what he did for free schools in Nova Scotia.
Nova Scotia did not derive its legislative authority from the British North America Act, as stated by the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent); it was constituted a province, with its own legislature, by royal charter years before the Province of Canada-Quebec and Ontario-was finally ceded to Britain. If my memory serves me correctly, it was so constituted back in 1757. It also had responsible government and it had a flag of its own. It is the only province or colony in the whole world which had that status. It had sovereign rights. Although not as large as some other territories, it had sovereign rights, and its part as regards the British North America Act justified it in believing that that was a treaty and that it had equal rights with the federal government in seeing that the conditions of that treaty were carried out down through the years.
The province of New Brunswick was constituted as a province, never as a colony, in 1784, with her own legislature and by royal charter.
Confederation had its genesis in Nova Scotia. The Charlottetown conference originated in Nova Scotia; the Quebec conference resulted from the conference at Charlottetown, the London conference from the Quebec conference, and the British North America Act from the London conference. I repeat, confederation had its genesis in Nova Scotia. Surely, if that is so, and in the light of history, that province has the right to be consulted at
Redistribution

such a time as this when a major change is being made in the constitution of Canada. I will read from the Journals of Nova Scotia, of February 4, 1864, from the King's speech opening the general assembly, paragraph (8):
The importance of consolidating the influence and advancing the common progress of the three maritime provinces, whose interests are so closely identified, has for some time attracted a large share of public attention, and I propose to submit for your consideration-
This is from the speech from the throne.
-a proposition in which the cooperation of the governments of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island will be invited with a view to the union of the three provinces under one government and legislature.
Here is a further minute from the Journals of Nova Scotia, general assembly, March 21, 1864, page 74:
The provincial secretary presented to the house the correspondence re union of the maritime provinces.
Then again, on March 29, 1864, at page 87:
The provincial secretary moved the following resolution, which was unanimously passed:
That an humble address be presented to His Excellency the administrator of the government requesting him to appoint delegates, not to exceed five, to confer with the delegates who were appointed by the governments of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island for the purpose of considering the subject of the union of the three provinces under one government and legislature, such union to take effect when confirmed by legislative enactment of the various provinces interested and approved by Her Majesty the Queen.
Again, on April 7:
The preceding resolution sent to the legislative council for concurrence . . .
And so on.
Nova Scotia made its full contribution to the formation of Canada and the development of the Dominion of Canada ever since. It participated in the cost of acquiring the Hudson's Bay company's lands, the purchase thereof, out of which lands the prairie provinces were formed. It sent troops to put down the northwest rebellion, and contributed its proportion to the cost of building the Canadian Pacific railway, and that great railway was never granted running rights into Nova Scotia. Nova Scotia's statesman, Sir Charles Tupper, supported by sixteen members from that province, advocated the national policy which was the foundation of industrial Canada, the basis upon which industrial Canada has been built up, under which this country made such remarkable achievements in the first great war and again in this recent great war, the pride of the whole of Canada. The very basis of this accomplishment was the national policy of 1878, which was sponsored by the public men of Nova Scotia.

Not only have we had war industries resulting from this industrial development; we have also the peace-time industries upon which the national income of the country depends. Moreover, the sons and daughters of Nova Scotia have gone to all parts of Canada, to the prairie provinces and to central Canada, to British Columbia, to assist in building up those sections. Just a few days ago the newspapers of Canada lamented the death of that great banker, that great Canadian, Morris W. Wilson, a native of Nova Scotia and head of The Royal Bank of Canada. He was succeeded by Sydney George Dobson, another great Nova Scotian, and they have as their associates other Nova Scotians, Mr. Enman of the Bank of Nova Scotia; Mr. Spinney of the Bank of Montreal; Mr. Logan of the Canadian Bank of Commerce; Mr. Elderkin, who is supervisor or inspector of banking in the Department of Finance, and many others. I mention this to indicate the contributions that Nova Scotians have made in the business life of Canada.
It was through the instrumentality of great statesmanship that Canada has developed and will last for centuries, for thousands of years. Nova Scotia had a prominent part in achieving confederation, and the province has supported all the great measures that have aided in building up Canada ever since. I believe that under a proper legal interpretation Nova Scotia should be consulted in any amendment to the B.N.A. Act. At any rate it would be only the part of decency that it should be consulted before any major amendment is made to the British North America Act, the very basis upon which our sovereign province came into confederation.
Surely our province is not simply to be sacrified in confederation. I consider it an obligation of all members of this house, from all parts of Canada, to see that Nova Scotia prospers in confederation and that her people are happy. That, unfortunately, is not so today. I believe that a special duty rests upon the leader of the Progressive Conservative party (Mr. Bracken), who inherits the responsibilities of his predecessors, to see that Nova Scotia and the maritime provinces generally are prosperous in our confederation. We get no political kudos because of discontent under confederation. Others do; we do not. We have to justify it, and I am proud to justify it. For better or for worse, we are part of Canada for all time. But I appeal to the house tp see that we have our place in confederation and share in the prosperity and happiness of the rest of Canada, and that Nova Scotia is consulted before any changes are made in the act under wdiieh we entered confederation.

My deskmate, the member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), pointed out in his able speech that there is no room for expansion geographically in the maritime provinces. There is none in Nova Scotia. That is not true of the other provinces. They have all expanded. There are many constituencies-I will not enumerate them-that were hot in existence at the time of confederation, some of them indeed not in existence at the beginning of this century, and they now have large populations which go to make up the total population of Canada.
Representation in Nova Scotia, since shortly after confederation, has gradually diminished. In 1867 Nova Scotia had nineteen members to 181 for all Canada, or one for Nova Scotia to 9-53 for all Canada. In 1882 Nova Scotia had twenty-one to 210, or one to ten for all Canada. In 1904 Nova Scotia had eighteen to 214, or one to 11-88. In 1925 Nova Scotia had fourteen out of 241, or one in 17-21. In 1945, the present time, Nova Scotia has twelve members out of 245, or one to 20-42 for all Canada. Under the British North America Act as it now stands, if it were not amended, Nova Scotia is entitled to twelve out of 238 or one in 19-83. It is unfortunate, and we lament it in Nova Scotia, that there was a reduction in our membership, but we accepted it census after census; but this is the first time that any of the western provinces have had to suffer, and they will not accept it as it was accepted in the maritime provinces.
According to the Canada Year Book, the population of Nova Scotia bore the following percentages to the population of the rest of Canada. In 1871, 10-51; in 1881, 10-19; in 1891, 9-32; in 1901, 8-56; in 1911, 6-83; in 1921, 5-96; and in 1931, 4-94 per cent. In 1941 we went up a little bit to 5-02 per cent. If that percentage were measured in the area that constituted original Canada I do not believe that our loss of percentage of population would have been one-half of what it is. It would show a far more favourable percentage if only the population of the original parts of Canada were taken into consideration.
Under this resolution Nova Scotia is offered an increase of one member. The membership will be increased from twelve to thirteen, but that is a fleeting concession. Personally I prefer not to accept it. Why? Because there is no permanency to it. Under the British North America Act, which Nova Scotia by sovereign right approved, it was possible to increase the membership as it was increased after different censuses in the prairie provinces and British Columbia, so that we did not suffer. But under this resolution introduced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) we have a fixed membership of 255. If Manitoba, or Quebec, or Ontario, or Saskatchewan, or Alberta, or British Columbia gets an increased number in the future, where is it to come from? It must come from the remaining provinces; and just as certain as we are discussing this resolution to-night it is going to come from Nova Scotia. If the trend of the past years continues not only will one come from Nova Scotia but two and three, and then we shall be down to the minimum of ten members out of 255, which violates, I believe, the legal rights of Nova Scotia; it violates the spirit of confederation. That is why I personally am not disposed to accept this increase of one member. There is no permanency to it under this resolution, because in the future the representation of all Canada will never be above 255. It must remain at that figure, and when there is an adjustment some of the provinces will suffer. I warn Saskatchewan and Manitoba that with their mass production machine age which appears to be taking place in the prairie provinces and with the days of the homestead being a thing of the past, they too may suffer as Nova Scotia has suffered in the past. New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island would suffer and we would likely go below ten members in the house if it were not for the amendment to the British North America Act which was put into effect under the government of Sir Robert Borden by which we could not have fewer members than that amendment provides for, which is ten for Nova Scotia, ten for New Brunswick and four for Prince Edward Island, although the population of Nova Scotia has always been and probably always will be larger than that of New Brunswick, we shall have the same minimum.
Poor old Nova Scotia down by the sea has suffered in some respects ever since confederation. I was reading some of the debates of previous years but I am not going to quote them to-night. In those debates I found that Mr. E. M. Macdonald, a prominent Liberal, said that Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island would never have entered confederation unless they were assured that they would be able to retain the membership which they had when they entered confederation.
This increase in membership to 255 is not going to be fair to Nova Scotia. I do not believe there is any justification for it in the British North America Act. I believe it violates sections 51 and 52 of that act, but it also imposes increased expenditures for the government of this country. I have been opposed to that. When I first entered the

Nova Scotia legislature twenty-one years ago we had a membership of forty-three, which we considered too large. We reduced it to thirty-seven; later we reduced it to thirty, and I believe they have got along just as well ever since. According to the last census in Nova Scotia, they are entitled to a redistribution of seats. If the basis of representation that we proposed at that time is followed I believe that there would be an addition of seven seats in that legislature. Anyway the electors of Nova Scotia felt that we were overgoverned and we reduced the membership. But that policy is not being followed here if this resolution becomes effective.
Under this resolution neither the electorate of Nova Scotia, nor the legislature, nor the government, nor the premier of that province is being consulted. There may be communications with the governments of the provinces, but, if so, they should be tabled in the house.
What was the basis of confederation? What did the fathers of confederation have in mind when the basis of representation was established? What would they say to-day? What stand would they expect me to take as a representative from Nova Scotia? I am just as sure as they enacted confederation that they would require that I speak for them, and no one	has	more right to speak	for	thefathers of confederation than I have. Four of them came from my native town of Amherst; one of them, a Liberal, is in my family tree. What would they say? They would say that this government has no right to attempt to put	into	effect an amendment	to	theBritish North America Act without consulting Nova Scotia. The government should stand not by	the	letter of the law but	by	thespirit of	what	was intended. Surely, over	the
years, from the time of confederation down to this day, Nova Scotia has earned the right to sympathetic consideration from public men from all over Canada and not the kind of treatment which appears to be attempted here.
What has been the attitude of the public men from Nova Scotia? I shall not quote them all, but I do not believe there is a single public man from Nova Scotia at any time, irrespective of his party, who in this parliament or on the floor of the legislature of Nova Scotia, would ever approve any changes in the British North America Act without the sovereign province of Nova Scotia being consulted. I am sure that Sir Robert Borden did not. What he said has been

quoted here by previous speakers, and it would not be out of place for me to quote him again. This was on February 10, 1914:
Speaking for myself, I do not see how it would be possible for this parliament to attempt any alteration in the representation of the provinces without the consent of the provinces *themselves.
What did the Hon. Layton Ralston say, the hero of two wars, the man we saw walk the plank here because he stood for duty? He supported the stand taken by the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, that the provinces should be consulted. I need not quote what he said. What did Viscount Bennett say when he was Prime Minister of this country? What were his actions? What stand did he take in 1931, when legislation affecting the merchant shipping legislation was being enacted in Great Britain? Here is a record of the stand taken by Mr. Bennett and his associates. On February 23, 1931, Mr. Bennett issued an invitation to the provincial governments to meet the federal representatives at a dominion-provincial conference to consider the statute of Westminster in 1929, which was the outgrowth of the imperial conference of 1926. This was a conference on the operation of dominion legislation and merchant shipping legislation. The meeting was held in Ottawa on April 7 and 8, 1931, and the delegates agreed that the following sections should be inserted in the statute of Westminster :
1.	Nothing in this act shall be deemed to apply to the repeal, amendment or alteration of the British North America Act of 1867 to 1930 or any order, rule or regulation thereunder.
That is specific. Other recommendations were:
2.	The powers conferred by this act upon the parliament of Canada or upon the legislatures of the provinces shall be restricted to the enactment of laws in relation to matters within the competence of the parliament of Canada or of any of the legislatures of the provinces respectively.
3.	The provision of the section (relating to the Colonial Laws Validity Act) of this act shall extend to the laws made by any of the provinces of Canada and to the powers of the legislatures of such provinces.
I continue reading the report of that conference:
Once more the provinces weTe attempting to safeguard their rights. Mr. Bennett promised the delegates that at a near future date he would summon a conference on constitutional issues with the purpose of considering any further amendments to the British North America Act.
Actions speak louder than words, and those were the actions of Mr. Bennett and his associates. But those are not the actions of

the present able Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) or the government and party which are going to support him and make this a political issue. This never should become a political issue. As I said earlier, confederation came about through the combined efforts of the leading men of all parties; but, as the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) said, this is being treated in the light of "political expediency". I have one more quotation to offer; it is a statement by the late Hon. Norman McL. Rogers.

He was private secretary-and an able one-to the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). Later he was Minister of Labour and, still later, Minister of National Defence, which position he occupied when he met his untimely death. I do not know whether he was in the Prime Minister's office at the time he made this statement, but he was arguing against the theory that it wras necessary in law to consult the provinces. It would appear that federal practice and political expediency call for a limited measure of provincial consultation and consent in the future amendment to the Canadian constitution, and for definite guarantees with respect to the rights of certain minorities.
I could also quote Hon. E. M. Macdonald, who at different times went on record as stating that the provinces should be consulted with respect to any amendment of the British North America Act.

He was Minister of National Defence at one time. I am going to repeat what I said earlier, that there is not a single instance on record of any public man in Nova Scotia, irrespective of politics, admitting that the British North America Act, under which that province entered confederation, can be amended without consulting the province; and, if I can speak for Nova Scotia, I say that such amendment should not be adopted and put into effect unless that province is at least consulted and, I believe, until it has approved. I have quoted certain public men. What do the leading newspapers of that province say? Without exception they are opposed to this form of redistribution at the present time. I quote from the Halifax Herald 'of June 8, which said:
This redistribution will be carried out on the basis of the decennial census of 1941-but, if the 1941 census was undesirable as a basis for redistribution in 1943, how can it be made desirable and fair and satisfactory and efficient by any plan that may be brought forward now? That aspect of the matter may rest for the moment.
What really counts is this: if government and parliament are to go ahead with the present plan, then they will not be getting down -to the roots of the situation at all.
The present plan may be criticized on the grounds of basic census figures ... it may be criticized because the provinces may not be consulted respecting the necessary constitutional amendment ... it may be criticized because it is unfair to one province and unduly "fair" to another . . .
Then it goes on to quote the Prime Minister of this country, supporting what he advocated some years ago. The Herald continues:
What Canada needs, of course, is a modern and efficient measure of electoral reform to replace an archaic system producing undemocratic and impossible results . . . The present prime minister made this positive declaration more than ten years ago: "I am in favour of the alternative vote and am also in favour of proportional representation."
I need not quote more of that editorial, and there are several others along the same lines. I would refer to the editorial in the Halifax Chronicle of June 3. I am not going to read it all; it is too long, but it says:
There has been very little demand for redistribution at this time ... it takes second place now -to more pressing problems. Most Canadians are waiting with anxiety for a budget already long overdue. We have a fuel crisis on our hands, and the prospects for next winter demand that greater attention be given immediately to the formulation of a national policy for native coal.
. . . the need for additional housing is still acute . . . We need, too, a far more serious consideration of industrial reconstruction and the upsurge of labour unrest -that is shackling efficiency . . . Taxes, housing and strikes are the things that need the .first attention at the moment ... If we must have a redistribution bill, why must it be one -that increases the membership of the house?
. . . Yet an increase in house representation means an increase in taxation. If the proposed bill goes through as presented, it will cost the country a minimum of an additional $60,000 a year in salaries and allowances for the new members.
If on the other hand we were to allow one member for each 50,000 people, reducing -the number of seats to 233, there would be an annual saving of $72,000, or of $132,000 if the proposed bill bringing total representation up to 255 is passed.
The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) elaborated on that point in his excellent address the other evening. The Chronicle goes on:
Such economies may sound small business in a country where we have a government accustomed to talk in billions. Yet economy must begin somewhere, and before this bill is debated opinion might well be canvassed as to whether its provisions look in the right direction.

I could quote from the Sydney Record-Post and other Nova Scotia newspapers, but I shall not delay the house by so doing. I may add, that many newspapers all across Canada are expressing the same view.
The Minister of Justice, in his able speech when presenting this resolution, made the following statement:
Another question, which has arisen each time there has been any move to ask for an amendment of the British North America Act, has been whether or not the provinces had been consulted and had agreed to it, I think that when the question is put in that form it is ambiguous. The provinces, that is to sav the people of the provinces, are all represented in this parliament, and for the purposes of such matters as are confided to the jurisdiction of this parliament it is by those representatives here that the people of the provinces speak.
I am a representative from Nova Scotia. Four of the fathers of confederation came from my home township. I have not been consulted. None of my colleagues has been called into consultation. The Minister of Justice has not called me into consultation, and I do not believe that members from Nova Scotia, as a body, have been consulted. Some of them, more subservient than the hon. member for New Westminster, may support the government because of "political expediency." I shall now quote from the remarks of the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell). He said that he does not think we should be consulted in Nova Scotia. Speaking on June 6, as reported at page 2235 of Hansard, he said:
Therefore X suggest to the hon. member that if this parliament decides that something should be done in the interests of all the people of Canada, and it is within its constitutional right to do so, the will of this parliament should prevail.
I question that statement; I disagree with it. If I have a voice to represent the feelings of the people of Nova Scotia, a voice which comes down from 1864, when confederation had its very beginning in Nova Scotia, then I say he does not represent the views of that province.
