speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to discuss the constitutional question which has been raised by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, for the very good reason . that no'doubt, as the debate proceeds, the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) will deal with that question in his usual competent manner.
I do, however, wish to answer on the basis of the position taken by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), namely, that one in the house should speak for his constituency or for his province, and feel free to do so without arguing any notions he may have with regard to the necessity for unity in Canada. I can speak to-night with the unanimous consent of all political parties represented in the legislature of Saskatchewan, when I say that they are not interested in having the government of that province consulted on this particular matter.
I state that advisedly, because I was just reading the Regina Leader before I came to the chamber, and noticed that in interviews given the press by the premier of Saskatchewan and by the leader of His Majesty's opposition in that province, both had agreed with the principle of the resolution introduced
by the Minister of Justice, and both had suggested that it would not be necessary for an appeal to be made to that province. It is not necessary for me, coming from Saskatchewan, to discuss the constitutional question as it is related to this issue, that is, that the provinces ought to be consulted when an amendment of this kind is being asked for.
The suggestion was made a few moments ago that this question has been raised because of political expediency. I do not know just what was meant by that suggestion, but I would say that the question has been raised on this occasion for a very different reason from that which caused the raising of a similar question in days gone by. If one goes back to the days preceding confederation and reads the history of that time he will agree that there was a great deal of discontent, lack of unity and discussion of questions largely from the point of view of local community interest, with the result that, after conferences had been held and discussions had taken place, the act of confederation, or the British North America Act, was passed with the object of bringing about a condition of unity as among the provinces, or as among the colonies which then constituted the maritime provinces and what we sometimes speak of now as the central part of Canada, namely, Ontario and Quebec.
It was only natural that at that time very little discussion should take place related in any way to what we know to-day as the prairie provinces or very little discussion, in the initial stages at least, in so far as British Columbia was concerned. The discussion largely had to do with the differences of opinion that had existed among the colonies in the eastern part of Canada, and so the provisions of the British North America Act in relation to this matter, as well as to other matters, had to do largely with the discussions which had taken place in what is to-day Ontario, Quebec and the three maritime provinces.
Therefore, I was not at all surprised when the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black), who has just taken his seat, made the statement that the discussions as to redistribution that had gone on were carried on by members from the maritime provinces and from the two central provinces, but that very little had been heard from the western provinces until such time as it became necessary to reduce the seats in western Canada under the system of redistribution which is provided for in the act. I do not agree with the hon. member when he says that the maritime provinces always took without any protest, the decisions which were brought about by the terms of confederation. As a matter of fact, the chief reason for the
Redistribution

discussions which are now taking place in the house is the fact that an amendment was made to the constitution in 1915 to provide against the representation in the maritime provinces dropping below the numbers which represented them in the senate. For that reason Prince Edward Island at the present time has four members instead of two; New Brunswick is protected with its membership of ten, the act providing that it cannot go below that number, and Nova Scotia, with a present membership of twelve, is protected by the act against that membership dropping below ten.
If there were any provinces in the Dominion of Canada that have a right to protest against that amendment it is the western provinces, beginning with Manitoba and extending to British Columbia. Why? The only protection we have under that clause is the protection which says that, no matter if our population be twice the population of Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick, we shall have six members for each province. Your population as compared with that of Canada drops to those proportions. All we are entitled to under the constitution is twenty-four senators from the four western provinces, which gives us a membership of six in each. If there are any protests that should be made about the provisions which were placed in the statute because of the protests made by the maritime provinces, they ought to come from the western provinces. But up to the present time we have not made any protest. The hon. member for Cumberland has invited protests along that line when he intimates that in the past the maritime provinces have taken the constitution as it is, but that immediately the membership of the western provinces comes under consideration -we want the constitution amended. Well, the constitution has been amended before and the protection given which I have indicated.
There is one other feature of the discussion to which I should like to call attention. We have been in the habit in this country of discussing everything from the point of view of its effect upon Ontario and Quebec. That is natural because, as we go back and read Hansard, we find that it was in connection w'ith the representation of those two provinces that most of the discussion took place. When we quoted matters with regard to redistribution we were led naturally into a discussion of representation in the province of Quebec or representation in the province of Ontario. Perhaps that has been given undue emphasis on this occasion, not only in this house but outside the house.

This is not a proposal coming from the province of Quebec. It so happens that the Minister of Justice, in his most capable manner, introduced the resolution because he is the Minister of Justice, but the fact that he comes from the province of Quebec does not indicate that this was a suggestion by the province of Quebec. No one is hurrying redistribution at the present time. Under our constitution redistribution should have taken place in 1943, prior to the last election. We amended our constitution to provide that it should not take place then. It was stated at that time that redistribution would take place in- the earliest possible session after the war. I venture to say that if that had not been provided in 1943 the proposal to postpone redistribution would not have passed this house. It was insisted that redistribution should be brought into this house in the first possible session after the war was over, so that now in 1946 we are discussing redistribution, in the first full session after the end of the war.
That being the case, may I say that two important matters are involved. The first is the fact that in the early constitution it was provided that a province had to vary its population by one-twentieth before its membership could be reduced. As a result of that, Ontario is entitled to possibly eight more members than it would be under a simple basis of representation by population. What was the issue raised in 1943 by those who came from the province of Quebec? It was not based on the proposal which is being made at this session. The contention was that Quebec had been used from the time of confederation down to the present time as the province in which the basis of constituency representation would be figured. In other words, you take the population of the province of Quebec and divide it by sixty-five, and you get the representation for each constituency in that province, and then you divide the population of the other provinces by that unit in order to get the representation in the other provinces.
The constitution sets sixty-five members for the province of Quebec, and the province of Quebec said in effect in 1943, "We have had that condition now since the time of confederation. We would like to suggest that Ontario be taken as the province where the unit is determined; that our population be divided by whatever that unit is, and that we proceed from now on with that as the basis of our redistribution in Canada." That has stood in my mind from that time down to the present as the proposal which was made by those who represented Quebec in the

Redistribution
house at that particular time. But that is not the proposal which is contained in this resolution. If anyone is looking for the reason for the suggestion that the old provision be removed one does not have to think in terms of political expediency; one should think in terms of what the constitution was really intended to bring about in the first place, namely unity among the people of this country. It seems to me that if we want to have unity in Canada one of the first things to be done is to remove the necessity of any discussion whatsoever as to any different relationship at between Ontario and Quebec, or as to the relationship existing between any other province in Canada and Quebec, or between any other province in Canada and Ontario. So that it has been thought wise in bringing down this resolution to remove all reference to any of the provinces in so far as that particular point is concerned and to make it possible for us to figure out a unit for representation which is based upon the population of Canada. If we were going to submit to the condition which was raised a few moments ago by the hon. member for Cumberland; if we had intended to create the condition which he has outlined as existing, then of course we would not have done what is contained in this resolution. He has suggested that by some means or other Nova Scotia can be reduced below ten members under this resolution, and that New Brunswick can be reduced below ten members. Well, he has not read the resolution carefully, or he would know that Nova Scotia can never at any time under this resolution be reduced below ten, and that New Brunswick can never be reduced below its present ten.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: If the minister will allow me, I did not make that statement. I said that this would be taken as a precedent; that further amendments may be made, without consulting the maritime provinces, which would result in a further reduction of our membership.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Well, of course, if we are to take under consideration all the possibilities of what any house of commons or any parliament in Canada might do, and make them as ridiculous as some people think they might be, we would be warranted in following an argument of that kind. But the fact of the matter is that the only reason that this question could not be stated in the resolution in the simplest possible form is for the purpose of retaining the protection which Nova Scotia has and retaining the protection which New Brunswick has. If it had not been for that consideration, all that it
w'ould have been necessary to say in order to make plain to the people of Canada what is intended would be this: "We are going to deduct the population of the province of Prince Edward Island and of the Yukon Territory and of the Northwest Territories from the whole population of Canada; then divide the remaining number by 250, and so get your unit; then divide the populations of each province by that unit of population, and we will get the membership for each province, and the total membership in these provinces will be 250, and then we will add back on the five that we have already taken off from Prince Edward Island and the Yukon, and you will have 255." There w'ould have been no necessity of saying anything more than that, had it not been for the fact that some day Nova Scotia may drop below a figure which would entitle it to ten members. If it ever does, then instead of subtracting five members we will subtract fifteen, and we will also subtract the population of Nova Scotia and of Prince Edward Island and of the Yukon Territory from the population of Canada and divide by the number which is left, which in that case would be 240, and you get your unit. When the seven provinces are provided with 240 members, the fifteen are added back in to make the total of 255. In other words, the resolution absolutely provides that the membership of this house can never be more than 255 so long as the meaning of this resolution is put into a bill and passed first by this parliament and then by the British parliament. That is what is being asked for.
Someone suggested this evening that if we went on the same basis as they have in the United States we would have a very much smaller house than we have here at present. I would ask my hon. friend to let his mind go back to the time when the United States had a population of only twenty-five million, and take his figures, based upon the membership of the houses then, and divide them into the population and see what he would have got. This resolution provides for an amendment to the constitution which retains the membership of the House of Commons at exactly the same figure when we have forty million people as it provides for at the present time when we have less than twelve million people. In other words, the membership of the house would not under this resolution ever increase beyond 255. It would remain at that throughout all time until someone undertook to amend the constitution further in order to provide for something else. But we in this parliament cannot take into consideration all the things which people may
Redistribution

do fifty years hence, or all the things they may do even twenty years hence. We can only act in the light of the information and the knowledge we have and do the thing which we think advisable. Under this resolution what we are proposing as advisable is to have the House of Commons composed of 255 members, and we are providing the means under which it will not increase beyond that figure but will remain at it.
I wanted to make that plain. But there is another thing I wanted to say in relation to this. The hon. member for New Westminster seems to base his opposition to the resolution upon the suggestion that Saskatchewan and perhaps some of the other prairie provinces are going to benefit by this being done now, and that probably British Columbia is going to lose something by this being done now. If he intended to argue from that that the prairies had something to do with proposing the plan I will agree. I can not understand his computations on the figures which are available. If we are going to follow what he has suggested, namely do nothing until after 1951, when the next census will be taken, British Columbia would remain with two members less than are provided for under this resolution and Saskatchewan would remain with one member more than is provided for under this resolution. In other words, Saskatchewan would remain at twenty-one until 1951, and British Columbia, with what he says is a greater population than Saskatchewan-and I do not admit that-would have a representation of only sixteen, not eighteen. So that if we want to do something at the present time in favour of British Columbia in order to give it a representation which is more comparable with the representation which Saskatchewan has, I would suggest that this resolution does it to much better advantage than the suggestion made by the hon. member for New Westminster. He would still maintain in his province a representation of eighteen until the next census, and we would retain in Saskatchewan only twenty until the next census is taken. I find it a little difficult to follow his reasoning to the effect that it would be twenty-five years longer before the C.C.F. would get into power in Canada under this scheme than under some other. I do not believe they will ever get into power under any scheme, though that is a matter of opinion. That, I think, has little bearing on the question which is under discussion.
I do not believe that the hon. member for New Westminster has justified the position which he says he is to take. If he is thinking in such terms as he indicated, in terms first of the welfare of his constituency and then

of British Columbia, under this proposal his constituency might be smaller than it is now, but I do not know whether that would help him. But under this proposal British Columbia would certainly have two members more than under his proposal until the next redis-tiibution, in which case that province, I think, would be more fully represented here than otherwise it would be.
I am inclined to agree when he suggests that British Columbia is on the up-grade in the matter of increased population. I am not sure that Saskatchewan is on the down-grade in matters of population. We have been on the down-grade for some time in other respects but not necessarily in population. Probably the fact that we were on the down-grade in matters of population for two or three years had something to do with some other things that have happened in Saskatchewan during that period of time, but I do not believe that we are always going to have that government, and I do not think we shall always have the reasons for population being down that we have had during those two or three years. Looking at the western provinces, I have always felt that Saskatchewan had a great deal to be proud of, and one fact that she has had a great deal to be proud of is that she has always had a greater population ever since people began to go there and to learn of conditions in Saskatchewan. She has always had a greater population than the other western provinces.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Not now.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Oh. she still has, just by about the margin of two members that are being allowed under this resolution. We may have to wait until 1951 to be able to prove it, but in the meantime we are taking it for granted that the condition which is shown by every past census taken is still the position, that Saskatchewan has a greater population than any of the other western provinces, and one of the reasons why that has been the case in the past is this. People tell me, "Look at the undeveloped natural resources they have in the foothills of the Rocky Mountains".
I agree with people who call attention to that fact. But in the next breath they say that Saskatchewan has nothing like the resources they have in the foothills of the Rockies. Let me say this. More real wealth has come out of any similar extent of territory in Saskatchewan. without any foothills; more real wealth has come out of any similar number of square miles in that province, than will ever come our of areas in mining districts where mining is the main reason for the development of any such area

Redistribution
We have an agricultural province. We depend upon the top six inches of soil; and if anyone takes a pencil and figures out the wealth that is coming out of that top six inches-the wealth that has come out ever since the province was first developed up to the present time-he will find it difficult to discover any other part of the world where a similar amount has been taken out of the natural resources of the country in order to provide for a similar number of people to live therein. That is the chief reason we have always had a higher population up to date.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Up to date.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Up to date, yes. My friends over the mountains think they will have a greatly increased population and I wish them ruck, because if they get a greatly increased population in British Columbia and Alberta and a greatly increased population along the foothills of the Rockies on the east side, then I may tell them that three-fifths of the cultivated farm lands in Canada arc located between the foothills and the city of Winnipeg. If any area is going to benefit by the fact that there are more people living in British Columbia, more people living in the foothills in Alberta, that area rvill be an agricultural area, and the greatest and best agricultural areas in western Canada are in Saskatchewan. I believe that as their population goes up ours will go up, and I hope their goes up very fast, because the faster it goes up, the sooner we shall be able to overtake anything that they are entitled to in the way of representation in this house.
I wanted to say these few words with regard to the situation as it exists, in order to emphasize the fact that this is not a Quebec proposal but a western proposal. I wish to make this appeal to members of the house and to those outside. This is not a question which concerns the maritimes alone. This is not a question which concerns the province of Quebec alone. This is not a question w'hich concerns Ontario alone, nor does it concern the province of British Columbia alone; and to make this statement-in spite of what the hon. member for New Westminster says-that a member in this house should discuss public questions from the point of view of his own constituency and his own province, is to say that we shall never have unity in this country so long as we have a membership here that speaks only from that point of view.
What we want in connection with redistribution is a constitution which thinks the necessity for considering Ontario as against Quebec, Quebec as against Ontario, the maritimes as
against western Canada, and western Canada as against some other part of the country, is entirely out of the picture. In order to take these questions entirely out of it there are two things to be done. One is to remove from the constitution any provisions that deprive us of the opportunity to have representation in this house according to population, with one exception, that exception being the provision which protects the maritime provinces against a reduction of membership until industry with population returns.
I am not so pessimistic about the maritimes as the hon. member for Cumberland. I do not agree that there cannot be a greater population in the maritimes. I believe that there is no part of Canada that has been dealt with more harshly by a policy which has built up central Canada at the expense of other parts of the dominion than the maritime provinces, and one .of the reasons for that is illustrated right in the city from which my hon. friend comes.
I have gone to his city. The first time I drove through Amherst I wondered what I was looking at-one of the finest little cities in the dominion, a city which a few years ago was one of the most prosperous industrial places in Canada A gentleman,-my hon. friend knows him Very well,-a good Irishman with the Irishman's usual wit, was driving me around the city, and I said to him, "How does it happen that I can see right through that building? I can see the windows on the other side." He answered, "Because everything has been taken out of it." I asked him who had taken it out and he said, "Those fellows in central Canada. They came to the conclusion that they could make something cheaper there than we could make it in Amherst; so somebody came here, bought the plant and closed it up, and now in central Canada they are making what we want to utilize here." He took me to one plant after another that was closed, and then finally said, "Here is one that is still operating." I said, "AVhat are they making in there?" He said, "Coffins." Well, there is something in an illustration of that kind. What we want in Canada in order to protect us against that kind of thing is not a different kind of redistribution bill, but something entirely different. That thing which would be entirely different could put the maritime provinces back on the map industrially. I wish to say to my hon. friends from the maritime provinces that I do not know of any way of bringing it about quicker than to 'have those provinces think more in terms of the development of western Canada than they have been doing,
Redistribution

and in thinking in those terms to believe that there are the possibilities of entering western Canada by more than one route.
Over a considerable part of the year, western Canada can be entered by water through Churchill. As we get the improvements to navigation which have come about during the war applied, western Canada will be entered for a greater number of months of the year than at the present time. The maritimes can operate into Hudson bay with boats and put their products the same distance from every prairie farmer at Churchill as they are putting them to-day at Fort William.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Does the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) agree with that, because only a short time ago he told us that two and a half months was the limit for the port of Churchill.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is an engineer. He built the elevators at Churchill; he had something to do with building some of the other equipment. He knows more about that question than I do; but in addition to that, being an engineer, he is going to be on the safe side. Being an optimist, and one who looks to the future, I do not need to look at it that way. I believe that with the improved facilities in navigation which we have, if we could navigate into Churchill for two and a half months at the time the elevators were built and at the time these investigations were made, then unless everything that we have heard about atomic energy and everything new is wrong, we ought to be able to operate into that port for at least a month longer, and I would hope for even more than a month longer. Whether we can or can not, in two or two and a half months the maritime provinces, manufacturing as they ought to be manufacturing, sitting right on the edge of the seas as they are, with ports unmatched in any part of Canada, ports open all the year round into which they could take the commodities of the world and manufacture them into the things that Canadians in the central part of Canada need, if they have the kind of vision as to what this country can become, they will have plants running twelve months of the year, and they can ship all the products that are required in western Canada in a year, in the months that the port of Churchill is open. If they cannot get it in through Churchill I am sure they can still navigate boats up the St. Lawrence and through the great lakes, and have just as much more come up by that route.

They do not need to be always saying that the central part of Canada has ruined the maritime provinces. I am going to say to them that I do not understand why this war did not bring more industries to the maritime provinces than it did. I do not understand why the war did not bring more industry to Alberta than it did. It brougth a lot more industry to British Columbia than they had before, and that is why they are optimistic. But I do want to say that I believe the people themselves had more to do with getting that industry into British Columbia than anyone else. I do not know of any place in Canada where the people right on the spot did less to get industry into it than did some sections of the maritimes and Alberta. Let me repeat, there are no sections of Canada which have a greater future industrially, if brains and capital, if you like, are applied to their possibilities, than the two extreme ends of this country, the maritime provinces and British Columbia, and the foothills of Alberta. They are the gates of the country. By developing the possibilities of these routes I have been speaking about, and the possibilities of the natural resources located in their areas, they can make it possible for greater and greater populations to live in those areas.
Why, we talk of this country as though it consisted only of the St. Lawrence river basin and only the half of it on the north side. This country consists of an area which is driving farther north all the time. It was that area which made possible the production of equipment during war time, and which makes possible the production of equipment now. These cities along the St. Lawrence could not exist at all with their present populations were it not for the enormous wealth contained in the back areas of the provinces of Quebec, Ontario and on into the prairies. Let me repeat, give us the industrial population to which we are entitled, first in the maritimes, because they are older, and then in Alberta and British Columbia, and we of Saskatchewan and the other prairie provinces will show you a prosperity which will match anything that has taken place in Canada down to the present time.
Tell us that there is no future for this country, that we can never have a population of more than twenty million and that we are going to have only a few millions in 1990, and proceed from that basis and this country will die on its feet. What we want in Canada today is vision. If the people who live in those areas feel that they are not getting what is coming to them, applying that vision will put those areas over, and by putting them over-
